about_this_instance.heading: About this instance
about_this_instance.lede: What this Morphit instance claims about itself, so you can check.

error.fetch_failed: Couldn't fetch this instance's verification info.

integrity.explain: This site serves {count} files. verify.json, linked below, lists each one with its hash — that list is the operator's own claim. The files that start the app (page shell, service worker, entry code) are also listed, with their hashes, in the latest release @morphit signed on the Blurt blockchain. When this site runs that signed version, your browser fetches each of those files from it and compares it with the signed hash. That catches a file changed by accident, by a partial break-in or on its way to you. It cannot protect you from the operator itself, who serves this check too.
integrity.check_mismatch: Only {matched} of {total} signed files match release {version} — this site serves changed files
integrity.check_not_checked: Not checked: this site runs version {running}, the latest signed release is {version}
integrity.check_no_release: Not checked: the signed release could not be read
integrity.check_incomplete: Not completed: a signed file could not be read from this site
integrity.check_unconfirmed: Not checked: the newest signed release could not be confirmed (the only one read is version {version}, older than this site's {running}). Checked again within the hour.

asset_stance.explain: Morphit is a federated marketplace. Every operator chooses which tradable assets their instance accepts new orders for — the default is everything in the canonical registry, but an operator can disable any trade-only asset (e.g. USDT) if they prefer their instance to specialize in privacy-first or decentralization-first assets. This is YOUR instance's current stance. Federation note: orders posted on other instances still appear in your orderbook regardless — the gate is only on new orders posted FROM here.
asset_stance.disabled_none: None — this instance accepts every tradable asset.
asset_stance.disabled_suffix: (operator-disabled on this instance; tradeable on peer instances)
asset_stance.federation_note: Want a different stance? Browse /operators to find an instance whose policy matches your preference, or run your own — see /run-a-node.

worried.explain: Morphit is federated — anyone can stand up an instance. If this one seems off, move to one you trust. Your keys, orders, and reputation live on the underlying chain, not on any single instance. You will see the same marketplace from anywhere.
worried.faq_pointer: For more on how to spot a bad operator, see
worried.compare_tool_pointer: If you want to compare what this instance shows against another, try the
worried.type_warning_heading: Type these into your browser bar — don't click
worried.type_warning_body: If you suspect this instance is rogue, the links here can't be trusted either — a hostile instance can render visible text saying "morphit.io" while the underlying URL points elsewhere. Type the addresses by hand into a clean browser tab.

payment_stance.explain: Every operator also chooses which payment methods their instance offers. The default is every method in the canonical registry; an operator can turn off any of them — most often Barter (goods/services) — to keep their instance money-only or focused. This is YOUR instance's current stance. Federation note: orders from other instances that use a disabled method still appear in your orderbook; the gate is only on new orders posted from here.
payment_stance.disabled_none: None — this instance offers every payment method.
payment_stance.disabled_suffix: (operator-disabled on this instance; usable on peer instances)

about_this_instance.fee_recipient_unregistered: This instance's fees account @{account} is not in its operator's on-chain registration yet, so other instances in the federation hide orders paid in BLURT here and do not deliver first messages sent from here to their users. The operator fixes this by running sudo morphit-ops register on the server.

setup_wizard.heading: Configure your instance
setup_wizard.intro: This wizard helps you generate the configuration lines and CLI commands you need to customize this Morphit instance. Nothing on this page mutates your server — you'll copy the output into your morphit.env file or your terminal, then restart your services.

assets.heading: Listed assets
assets.intro: Choose which crypto assets your instance lists for trading. BTC, XMR, and BLURT are always enabled — federation depends on them.
assets.output_heading: Add this line to your morphit.env file
assets.output_subtitle: Then restart the indexer service: `docker compose restart indexer`
assets.locked_title: Federation depends on this asset — operators cannot disable it

payment.heading: Add a custom payment method
payment.intro: If your region uses a payment method we haven't added to the canonical list, you can publish it as an instance-specific addition. Other instances will see it labeled with this instance's name.
payment.key_help: Lowercase letters, digits, underscores only. Maximum 32 characters. This is permanent once broadcast — orders will reference it forever.
payment.key_error_format: Lowercase letters, digits, and underscores only
payment.key_error_reserved: Key collides with a canonical method — pick a different key
payment.name_help: The user-facing name. Usually a brand name — don't translate it.
payment.description_help: One or two sentences. Users see this when choosing payment methods.
payment.output_heading: Run this command on your server
payment.output_subtitle: From the directory where you installed Morphit, paste this into your terminal. You'll be prompted for the posting key file path.
payment.output_pending: Fill in the key, name, description, and category fields above to generate the command.
payment.remove_key_error_canonical: Canonical methods can't be removed via the per-instance mechanism

disclosure.heading: What this wizard does and does not do
disclosure.read_only: Read-only: this page generates config and CLI text but never mutates your server. Nothing changes until you paste the output and apply it yourself.
disclosure.no_auth: Open access: this page has no login requirement because it never mutates anything. Anyone can visit it. If that's not what you want, place it behind your reverse proxy's auth.
disclosure.restart_required: Service restart required: after editing morphit.env, restart the indexer service so the change takes effect. The payment-method CLI broadcasts to chain immediately — no restart needed for that.

payment_remove.heading: Remove a custom payment method
payment_remove.intro: If you previously added a payment method via the CLI and want to retire it, generate the remove command here. Canonical methods (PayPal, Wise, etc.) cannot be removed — they're project-wide.
payment_remove.key_help: The exact key you used when adding the method. Run `morphit-ops payment-method list` on your server to see your current additions.
payment_remove.output_heading: Run this command on your server
payment_remove.output_subtitle: From the directory where you installed Morphit. You'll be prompted to confirm before the chain op is broadcast.
payment_remove.output_pending: Enter the machine key of an instance-specific method to generate the remove command.
payment_remove.orders_safety: Existing orders that reference this method continue to display correctly after removal — the on-chain key persists in those orders' history. Remove just means new orders can't pick it.

payment_disable.heading: Offered payment methods
payment_disable.intro: Choose which payment methods your instance offers. Unchecking a method hides it from the post-order picker and the orderbook filter. Disabling Barter (goods/services) is the common case — some operators keep their instance money-only.

app.tagline: Buy and sell crypto, your way.

privacy_warnings.usdt_centralized: Two things to know about USDT before trading: Tether Inc. issues and administers USDT and has the technical ability to freeze addresses (and has used it). Transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BNB Smart Chain) — a property of those chains. Pick the asset that fits your trade.
privacy_warnings.usdc_centralized: Two things to know about USDC before trading: Circle issues and administers USDC and has the technical ability to freeze addresses (and has used it). Transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon) — a property of those chains. Pick the asset that fits your trade.
privacy_warnings.dai_partly_centralized: Three things to know about DAI before trading: (1) Unlike USDT and USDC, DAI's token contract has no admin-controlled freeze function — MakerDAO can't blacklist your address. This is a real decentralization advantage. (2) DAI is partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module, so Circle's freeze power over USDC indirectly affects DAI redemption when the PSM holds USDC. (3) Like all stablecoins, DAI transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum) — a property of those chains, no on-chain privacy. Pick the asset that fits your trade.

You'll need your 12-word seed phrase, your keyfile, or your Blurt key to sign back in. Your posting + memo keys will be wiped from this session.

backup_keys.title: Back up your keys
backup_keys.subtitle: This is the most important page on {brand}. Read it before you need it.
backup_keys.reality_lead: Morphit is non-custodial. Nobody — not us, not your operator, not any support agent anywhere — can help you recover your account if you lose your keys.
backup_keys.reality_body:
There is no 'forgot password' link. There is no 'verify with ID' process. There is no backup account on a server somewhere. Your keys exist in two places: this device (right now) and wherever you copy them to. That's the entire list.

Lose the keys, lose the account. Lose the funds. Lose the reputation you built from every trade. No exceptions, no appeals, no human on Earth can intervene.

This is the tradeoff for a service that does not, and cannot, seize your money or freeze your account. The same thing that keeps you safe from us keeps you exposed to your own mistakes.
backup_keys.reality_slogan: In the crypto world, YOU are the bank.
backup_keys.what_heading: What to back up, and how
backup_keys.seed_body:
Your seed phrase is a standard BIP-39 list of 12 words, generated during onboarding. Morphit turns it into your Blurt keys with its own published derivation step, so another BIP-39 wallet given the same words will NOT produce these keys: only Morphit (or another program that implements the same open-source derivation) can regenerate them. To use your account in another Blurt wallet, back up your WIF keys as well. The seed is your ultimate recovery inside Morphit.

If you didn't write it down during onboarding, it's gone. We cannot regenerate it. Your keys were derived from it before it was wiped from memory.
backup_keys.seed_tip_paper: Write it on paper. Two copies, stored in two separate physical locations.
backup_keys.seed_tip_steel: For amounts you care about, stamp it into a steel backup plate. Paper burns and gets waterlogged.
backup_keys.seed_tip_split: For larger balances, split it: first 6 words in one location, last 6 in another. Both halves together = full access. Neither half alone = nothing.
backup_keys.seed_tip_digital_warning: Never store the seed in email, cloud notes, screenshots, password managers synced to a cloud, or any app that can be remotely accessed.
backup_keys.keyfile_body: This keyfile is your private keys, encrypted with your device password. Download it now and store it somewhere separate from the device you're using. If you forget the password, the keyfile is useless — so treat the password as equally critical.
backup_keys.keyfile_locked_hint: Sign in first to download your encrypted keyfile. This page still works without signing in for the education.
backup_keys.keyfile_download_err_locked: Your session appears to be locked. Sign in to download your keyfile.
backup_keys.redundancy_body:
The crypto survivors are the ones who planned for fire, flood, death, and their own forgetfulness.

Two physical copies of your seed phrase in separate locations. At least one in a safe or safety deposit box. Consider an estate plan: how does a trusted heir find your keys if something happens to you? Write down the instructions separately from the keys themselves.

Redundancy costs you 10 minutes of effort. Its absence can cost you everything.
backup_keys.keyfile_body_posting_only: This keyfile is your private posting key, encrypted with your device password. Download it now and store it somewhere separate from the device you're using. If you forget the password, the keyfile is useless — so treat the password as equally critical.
backup_keys.redundancy_body_posting_only:
The crypto survivors are the ones who planned for fire, flood, death, and their own forgetfulness.

Two encrypted copies of your keyfile, kept in separate physical locations. At least one in a safe or safety deposit box. Consider an estate plan: how does a trusted heir reach your funds if something happens to you? Write down the instructions separately from the key itself.

Redundancy costs you 10 minutes of effort. Its absence can cost you everything.
backup_keys.antipatterns_heading: Common mistakes that cost people everything
backup_keys.anti_email: Emailing the seed phrase to yourself. Any breach of your email provider exposes it.
backup_keys.anti_cloud: Storing the seed in Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive. These are searched by automated malware, subpoenaed by governments, breached by attackers.
backup_keys.anti_photo: Taking a photo of the seed. Your photos sync to the cloud. Your phone gets stolen. The photo leaks.
backup_keys.anti_share: Sharing the seed with 'support' — ours, or anyone else's. Real support never, ever asks for your seed. Anyone who does is a scammer.
backup_keys.anti_support: Assuming someone can help you recover. They can't. We can't. Nobody can. This is the whole point of non-custodial.
backup_keys.faq_lost_keys: What happens if I lose my keys?
backup_keys.error_download_failed: Couldn't prepare your keyfile for download. Try again.

show_seed.heading: Show me my 12-word seed phrase
show_seed.body: If you didn't write your seed phrase down at sign-up, you can recover it here. We'll ask for your password before showing it.
show_seed.password_hint: Same password you use to unlock {brand} on this device.
show_seed.shoulder_warning: Make sure nobody is looking at your screen.
show_seed.locked_hint: Sign in first to view your seed phrase.

error.locked: You need to be signed in to view your seed phrase.
error.no_seed_posting_only: This account was imported with a posting key only — there's no seed phrase to show. Use the keyfile download below for backup.
error.no_seed_posting_active: There's no 12-word seed for this account, and there can't be. A seed derives your keys — it can't be built backwards from keys you already had. Your keyfile below is your backup, and it now contains both your Posting and Active keys.

paired.heading: Your keys live on your phone
paired.body: This desktop is paired with your phone, which holds your real keys. The sections below are about backing up keys that aren't on this device — they apply to the phone you paired with. Open {brand} on the phone and go to "Back up my keys" there.
paired.deeplink_hint: If your phone is nearby, the button below opens the right page on it directly.

backup_keys.keyfile_body_posting_active: Your keyfile now holds your Posting key AND your Active key, encrypted with your {brand} password. Keep a copy somewhere safe: it's the only backup of the Active key you just saved to this device. It does not contain your Owner or Memo keys — those stay wherever you keep them today.

set_password.heading: First, choose a password for your backups
set_password.body: You signed in with your seed phrase just for this session, so your keys are locked in this browser under a random password you have never seen. A keyfile made from that would not open with anything you know. Choose a password: your keyfile and “Show my seed” will use it. Nothing is saved to this device.
set_password.error_mismatch: The two passwords are not the same.
set_password.error_weak: That password is too weak. Use at least 12 characters.

message.placeholder_encrypted_paired: Encrypted message — open {brand} on your phone to read it.
message.placeholder_encrypted_failed: This message couldn't be decrypted on this device. It may be damaged or sent to a different recipient key.
message.peer_not_ready: This recipient hasn't opened Morphit chat yet. Once they do, your message will go through on retry.
message.not_confirmed_on_chain: Not confirmed on the blockchain — it may have been dropped. Tap Retry to send it again.
message.on_chain_not_accepted: On the blockchain, but not accepted for delivery — the recipient may not be taking messages from you right now. Sending it again would not change that.
message.session_locked: Your session is locked. Unlock and try again.
message.unrecorded_detail: This message reached you directly from the sender's server, but the blockchain never recorded it, so there is no permanent proof it was sent. If the sender's app reported it as not sent, they may send it again.
message.unrecorded_detail_own: This message was sent from another of your sessions, but the blockchain never recorded it, so there is no permanent proof it was sent. You can send it again.
message.sender_unverified: Sender not verified: this message came in an older format (or after a key change you haven't accepted), so it can't be proved that this person wrote it. Don't pay to an address in it without confirming it with them another way.

composer.locked_hint: Unlock your session to send messages.

acct_reminder.heading: Permanent.
acct_reminder.body: Account numbers in chat go on the blockchain forever. Proofread carefully before sending.

inbox.empty_body: Find a trader on the orderbook or a profile page and tap Message to start a conversation.
inbox.load_error_fallback: Couldn't reach the conversations server — showing conversations you've opened on this device. Try refreshing.

block.body: They will no longer be able to message you on Morphit. You can unblock them later from Settings.

unblock.title: Unblock @{peer}?

stranger_fee.heading: Send your first message to @{peer}
stranger_fee.explain: {brand} charges a small one-time fee for first-contact messages to new people. This discourages spam while letting real conversations start freely.
stranger_fee.one_time_note: You'll never be charged again for messaging @{peer}. The fee only applies to the first message between two people.
stranger_fee.pill_explain: You haven't messaged @{peer} before. A small one-time fee unlocks this conversation.
stranger_fee.pill_locked_hint: Unlock your session to pay and send.

error.quote_failed: Could not fetch the current network fee. Please check your connection and try again.
error.no_active_envelope: No saved active key found on this device. Save your keys from Settings first, then try again.
error.broadcast_failed: Payment could not be broadcast. Your fee has not been spent. Please try again.
error.bad_password: That password did not unlock the active key.

escalation.heading: Fee escalated to {multiplier}× — you've messaged {count} stranger(s) in the last {window} minutes.
escalation.body: Please slow down. People dislike unsolicited contact, may block you, and blocks are visible on-chain — multiple blocks against your account hurt your standing as a counterparty. Wait 5+ minutes between first contacts to reset to base.

security.pub_pin_tampered_same_ref: We couldn't safely send: this peer's chat-key record looks tampered. The chat key your indexer is reporting doesn't match what was published on-chain. Try a different Morphit instance, or ask the recipient to confirm their chat key out of band.
security.pub_pin_older_indexer_ref: We couldn't safely send: your indexer is reporting a chat-key record that's older than what you've already seen. That shouldn't happen on a forward-only chain. Try refreshing or switching to another Morphit instance.
security.pub_pin_chain_reports_none: We couldn't safely send: your indexer says this peer has a chat key, but the blockchain reports none. The indexer may be out of sync, or fabricating data. Try another Morphit instance, or wait and retry.
security.pub_pin_chain_older_than_pin: We couldn't safely send: the blockchain reports an older chat key for this peer than the one you've already seen. That's internally inconsistent. Try another Morphit instance or another blockchain endpoint.
security.pub_pin_malformed_indexer_response: We couldn't safely send: your indexer returned malformed data for this peer's chat-key record. The indexer may be running an older version or be misconfigured. Try another Morphit instance.

confirm.title: Chat Security
confirm.body: Do you want to stop being able to reread your own messages after you leave this chat? Your partner can still read them, and their encrypted form stays on the chain. Choose No to keep reading your own history, like a normal messenger.
confirm.current_keep: Right now: you keep a copy and can reread your own messages.
confirm.current_destroy: Right now: you don't keep a copy, so you can't reread your own messages after you leave.

pdf_reminder.title: Don't forget to export this chat to PDF
pdf_reminder.body: In this mode you can't reread your own messages after you leave (your partner still can). Save a PDF now if you want to keep a copy.

security.chain_unreachable: We couldn't reach the blockchain to check this peer's chat key, so the message wasn't sent. This is common on Tor and I2P, where connections take a while to build. Nothing is wrong — try again in a moment.
security.pub_pin_key_changed: Not sent: this person's chat key changed. That happens when they reset their keys — or when someone is trying to read your messages. Open ⋮ → Verify peer and compare the new safety number with them over another channel before you accept it.
security.accept_new_key: I compared it — accept the new key

chat.lazy_load_failed: Couldn't load the chat view. Refresh the page and try again.

address.address_invalid_btc: That doesn't look like a valid Bitcoin address.

address.memo_explain: The buyer must include this memo in their BLURT transfer so you can match the payment to this trade.
address.memo_required_explain: Paste this memo into the memo field of your BLURT transfer. Without it, the seller can't match your payment to this trade.
address.xmr_jitter_explain: Adds a tiny random amount (less than ~$0.0002) to make this transfer unique on Monero's chain. Defeats 'same-amount' correlation attacks. Recommended.

address.xmr_jitter_send_exact_hint: Tell your buyer's wallet to send this exact amount, including the long decimals.
address.xmr_jitter_off_warning_body: Round amounts are easier to correlate on the Monero chain. Leave jitter on unless you have a reason to send an exact figure.
address.address_placeholder_usdt: Tether address (matching the network you picked)
address.address_invalid_usdt: This address does not match the USDT network you picked. Double-check before sending — cross-network sends lose your funds.
address.address_invalid_bch: That doesn't look like a valid Bitcoin Cash address.
address.address_invalid_ltc: That doesn't look like a valid Litecoin address.
address.amount_jitter_explain: Adds a tiny random extra (small enough to be a trivial implicit tip) to defeat amount-correlation between your order and the on-chain transfer. Strongly recommended on transparent chains.
address.amount_jitter_will_send: Your buyer's wallet will send exactly:
address.amount_jitter_send_exact_hint: This precise amount breaks the link between your order book post and the on-chain payment.
address.amount_jitter_off_warning_body: Anyone watching the chain can match this exact amount to your order. Turn the randomizer on unless you have a specific reason not to.
address.reuse_warning_body: You shared this address from this device before. Reusing the same address across trades links them on the public chain. Consider deriving a fresh address from your wallet for this trade.
address.payjoin_explain: If your wallet supports PayJoin (BIP-78), paste its endpoint URL here. Buyers whose wallets also support PayJoin will use a cooperative transaction that breaks chain-analysis heuristics. No effect on wallets without PayJoin support.
address.payjoin_badge_tooltip: The seller's wallet supports PayJoin (BIP-78). If your wallet supports it too, opening this URI will negotiate a cooperative transaction that improves privacy.
address.address_invalid_dash: That doesn't look like a valid Dash address.
address.address_placeholder_usdc: USD Coin address (matching the network you picked)
address.address_invalid_usdc: This address does not match the USDC network you picked. Double-check before sending — cross-network sends lose your funds. Note that Ethereum, Base, and Polygon addresses all start with 0x and look identical at the format level.
address.address_invalid_dai: Not a valid DAI address shape (expected EVM 0x[40 hex]).
address.address_invalid_doge: That doesn't look like a valid Dogecoin address.
address.address_invalid_zec: That doesn't look like a valid Zcash address.

address.address_invalid_xrp: Not a valid XRP Ledger address.  Expected an address starting with r followed by 24-34 base58 characters (no destination tag in this field).
address.blurt_account_not_found: No Blurt account with that name exists.

funds_sent.modal_subtitle: @{peer} will see the amount and transaction ID you enter below.
funds_sent.txid_help: The unique fingerprint your wallet showed after sending. Most wallets call it a TxID, Transaction Hash, or Tx Hash. It looks like a long jumble of letters and numbers (64 characters). Tap any sent transaction in your wallet to find it.
funds_sent.txid_invalid: That doesn't look like a valid transaction ID.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_to: The transfer was sent to a different recipient than expected.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_from: The transfer was sent from a different account than the buyer claims.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_amount: The on-chain amount differs from the amount you asked for.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_memo: The on-chain memo doesn't match the requested memo.
funds_sent.verify_not_found: Transaction not found yet — give it a block or two.
funds_sent.verify_wrong_op: Transaction found but contains no matching transfer.
funds_sent.verify_rpc_error: Could not verify on chain (RPC unreachable).
funds_sent.self_verify_mismatch_to: Your wallet sent to a different account than expected.
funds_sent.self_verify_mismatch_from: The on-chain transfer's sender doesn't match your account.

verify_peer.title: Verify safety number
verify_peer.subtitle: Compare this 60-digit safety number with @{peer} over a channel you already trust (voice call, in person, another platform). If both of you see the same number, nobody swapped your chat keys.
verify_peer.locked: Unlock your account first to compute the safety number.
verify_peer.peer_not_ready: @{peer} hasn't published their chat key yet. Try again after they open chat once.
verify_peer.tamper_heading: Tamper detected — DO NOT continue chatting
verify_peer.tamper_body: The chat key the indexer served for this peer doesn't match what the chain says. This is a strong signal of MITM or compromise. Stop trusting this conversation until you understand why.
verify_peer.error_indexer: Couldn't fetch the peer's chat key from the indexer.
verify_peer.error_bad_key: The peer's chat key is malformed.
verify_peer.error_unknown: Couldn't compute the safety number. Try again.
verify_peer.compare_body: Read the 12 groups to your contact over a voice call, in person, or another trusted channel. Do NOT compare them in this chat. If even one digit differs, treat the conversation as compromised.
verify_peer.why_body: By default Morphit chat trusts the indexer to deliver the right chat key for your counterparty. A hostile indexer could substitute attacker-controlled keys and read your messages. The safety number is computed on your device: half from your chat key, half from theirs. If both of you see the same 60 digits, nobody swapped a key. This protects against key substitution only; it does NOT prove the person on the other end of your phone call is who they say they are.
verify_peer.error_chain_unreachable: Couldn't reach the blockchain to check this peer's key. This is common on Tor and I2P, where connections take longer to build. Nothing is wrong with the key — try again in a moment.
verify_peer.reverify_heading: The safety number is longer now
verify_peer.reverify_body: It used to be 8 words, which a hostile server could fake with enough computing power. If you compared the old words with someone, compare this number with them once more.
verify_peer.key_changed_body: @{peer}'s chat key is not the one you used before, so the number below is new. Compare it with them over another channel. Accept it only if it matches what they see — until then nothing is sent to the new key.
verify_peer.key_changed_accept: The numbers match — accept the new key

export.title: {brand} chat with @{peer}
export.subtitle: End-to-end encrypted conversation, anchored on the blockchain.
export.verify_body: Every message below is a permanent entry on the public Blurt blockchain, signed by the sender's account. The “Blockchain proof” code on each message is its transaction ID: anyone can paste it into a Blurt block explorer (for example, blocks.blurtwallet.com) to confirm that this account sent a message to the other at the stated time. The chain holds only the encrypted form, so a third party can confirm that a message was sent, by whom and when — not what it said. The text shown was decrypted with the keys of the account named above. This PDF is an ordinary file that can be edited; it is a record for you, not proof of the wording.
export.unrecorded_label: never recorded on the blockchain — this line cannot be verified
export.footer: {brand} chat record. Check that each message was sent, by whom and when, on a block explorer.

cheat_sheet.heading: {brand} cheat-sheet
cheat_sheet.intro: A one-page reference for the things grandmas keep mixing up. Print it and keep it next to the keyboard.
cheat_sheet.subtitle: Quick reference for everything you'll be asked while using {brand}.
cheat_sheet.footer: Morphit · morphit.io · open source · AGPL-3.0 · keep this paper safe.

section_identity.heading: Account name vs seed phrase vs password
section_identity.account_name_body: Your public name on the chain (e.g. @alice). Other people see this. Choosing a new one is permanent — costs ~3 BLURT.
section_identity.seed_phrase_body: 12 words. The ONLY way back into your account if you lose your device. Anyone who has them owns your account. Write them on paper, store somewhere safe.
section_identity.password_body: Just for THIS device, not the chain. Encrypts your seed in this browser. If you forget it, type your seed phrase to log in again. Different from the seed.

section_fees.heading: Listing fee vs network fee vs trade payment
section_fees.listing_fee_body: What {brand} charges to publish your order. Tiny — about 12.5¢ (USD-equivalent) if you pay in BLURT, or about 25¢ if you pay in BTC or XMR. Your first buy is free (an order worth at least $1). You enter amounts in your own currency — you never have to think in BLURT.
section_fees.network_fee_body: What the Bitcoin or Monero network charges to confirm a payment. Goes to miners, not {brand}. Varies — check the wallet you send from.
section_fees.trade_payment_body: The actual money you send (or receive) for the trade. {brand} never holds it — straight from buyer to seller, off-platform.

section_assets.heading: Supported tradable assets
section_assets.btc: Bitcoin. Most known. Public ledger — anyone can see who paid whom. Fees vary widely.
section_assets.xmr: Monero. Private — no one can see who paid whom. Fees usually low. The privacy choice.
section_assets.blurt: The token of the Blurt blockchain that Morphit runs on. Used to pay listing fees, post messages, sign orders.
section_assets.usdt: Tether stablecoin. Pegged 1:1 to USD. Trade across four networks: ERC-20 (Ethereum), TRC-20 (Tron), SPL (Solana), BEP-20 (BNB Smart Chain). Pick the network before sending — cross-network is unrecoverable.
section_assets.bch: BCH — Bitcoin Cash, transparent, decentralized, bigger blocks than BTC
section_assets.ltc: LTC — Litecoin, fast, low-fee Bitcoin fork (since 2011). Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Litecoin wallet (Electrum-LTC, Litewallet, hardware wallets); accepts L… legacy, M… modern P2SH, and ltc1… SegWit addresses.
section_assets.dash: DASH — Dash, fast-confirmation Bitcoin-family chain (since 2014). Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Dash wallet (Dash Core, Dash Electrum, hardware wallets); accepts X… P2PKH and 7… P2SH addresses. Optional PrivateSend mixing via masternodes — pre-mix before sharing the address for stronger privacy.
section_assets.usdc: USD Coin stablecoin. Centralized — Circle can freeze any address. Trade-only.
section_assets.dai: DAI — MakerDAO USD-pegged stablecoin. Multi-network (ERC-20/Polygon/Base/Arbitrum, all EVM). Trade-only. Partly USDC-backed.
section_assets.doge: DOGE — Dogecoin, transparent proof-of-work chain (since 2013), merge-mined with Litecoin. Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Dogecoin wallet (Dogecoin Core, MyDoge, hardware wallets); accepts D… P2PKH and 9…/A… P2SH addresses. No native privacy upgrade —
section_assets.zec: ZEC — Zcash, proof-of-work chain with optional zero-knowledge shielded transactions (Sapling + Orchard pools). Supports both transparent (t1/t3, base58, similar to Bitcoin's legacy addresses) and shielded (zs1/u1, bech32, hides sender/recipient/amount) addresses. Trade-only — cannot pay listing fees.
section_assets.arrr: ARRR — Pirate Chain.  Proof-of-work cryptocurrency with chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool (every transaction is private by construction).  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use a Pirate Chain wallet (Treasure Chest, Pirate.Black, Verus); only one address format exists (zs1 Sapling shielded, 78 chars — visually identical to Zcash Sapling).
section_assets.dcr: Decred. A coin whose holders vote on how it's run. Public ledger like Bitcoin, with an optional privacy mode in its wallet.
section_assets.sol: SOL — Solana.  High-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use a Solana wallet (Phantom, Solflare, Cake Wallet for SOL, Trust Wallet); 32-44 character base58 addresses.  Send native SOL — not wrapped SOL or SPL tokens.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.
section_assets.eth: ETH — Ethereum.  Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use an Ethereum wallet (MetaMask, Rabby, Frame, Rainbow, Trust Wallet); 42-character 0x-prefixed hex addresses.  Send native ETH — not wrapped ETH (WETH) or ERC-20 tokens.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.  ENS names not resolved — paste raw 0x addresses.
section_assets.xrp: XRP — Ripple.  Federated Byzantine Agreement consensus on the XRP Ledger.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use an XRPL wallet (Xaman/Xumm, Crossmark, Bifrost, GemWallet, Trust Wallet); 24-34-char base58 addresses starting with `r`.  Destination tags required when sending to exchange-hosted addresses (32-bit integer routing).  Accounts need ≥1 XRP base reserve to exist.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.
section_assets.barter: Barter — goods or services, not a coin. Price your wares in local currency, pick the crypto(s) you'll accept (e.g. XMR, BTC, DOGE), and describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms. The listing needs no crypto address; you settle in whichever accepted crypto the buyer picks. Trade-only on {brand}.

section_recovery.heading: If something goes wrong
section_recovery.lost_seed_body: There is no recovery path. {brand} has no copy. If you still have access to the device, move funds out NOW and start a new account.
section_recovery.lost_password_body: Click "Sign in" and choose "Import seed phrase". Type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.lost_device_body: On a new device, go to morphit.io, click "Sign in", choose "Import seed phrase", type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.suspect_compromise_body: Move funds to a new account immediately. Anyone with the seed has full control. There's no "freeze" button on a blockchain.

(Details: {detail})
broadcast_err.low_blurt: Broadcasting costs a small BLURT fee, and larger updates (an avatar, for example) cost more because the fee scales with size. Your account's liquid BLURT is too low to cover it. Add a little liquid BLURT to your account, then try again. (Chain: {reason})

compare.heading: Compare orderbooks
compare.lede: See if two Morphit instances are serving the same orderbook. Useful when you suspect an instance is hiding orders (censorship), or just want to confirm they agree.

input.label: Compare with another Morphit instance
input.hint: Paste the URL of a second Morphit instance (e.g. https://example.org).

results.heading: Comparison
results.interpretation: A small disparity is normal — the two instances may be at slightly different indexed blocks. A large or persistent disparity across refreshes is the real signal.

pane.in_both_note: Orders both instances agree on. Listed briefly — these are not the censorship signal.

url_error.invalid_scheme: URL must use http:// or https://.
url_error.bad_host: URL host is missing or too long.

error.same_instance: That's the same instance you are on. Pick a different one to compare against.
error.local_failed: Could not fetch that instance's orderbook: {reason}
error.remote_failed: Could not fetch {host}'s orderbook: {reason}. The remote instance may be offline, unreachable, or blocking this request.
error.fetch_threw: Couldn't reach {host}. Network error or the instance is offline.
error.local_timeout: The orderbook took too long to load. Try again in a moment.
error.unknown_instance: {host} is not a registered Morphit instance, so it can't be compared. Pick one from the instance list.
error.remote_unreachable: This instance could not reach {host}. It may be offline or unreachable from here right now; try again later.
error.remote_bad_answer: {host} answered, but not with a Morphit orderbook.
error.busy: Too many comparisons right now. Try again in a minute.

footer.snapshot_note: This is a one-shot snapshot; both sides may have changed in the seconds between fetches. Refresh a few times over a minute or two to see a persistent pattern.

verdict.agree_body: Across the orders both instances could be compared on, every one appears on both. {n} orders matched. Nothing is being hidden by {host} in the range checked.
verdict.differ_body: Some orders appear on only one of the two instances. Check the block gap first — if the instances are at different heights, the newest orders legitimately differ. A difference that survives several re-runs is the real signal.
verdict.inconclusive_body: Both instances returned a capped page of orders and the pages do not overlap, so there is no range in which both are known to be complete. Nothing can be concluded from this comparison.
verdict.malformed_heading: One instance sent an impossible answer
verdict.malformed_body: {host} says it has more orders but sent none of them. The first page of an orderbook that has orders always contains some, so this is how an instance hiding its orders would answer. Re-run in a few minutes; if it keeps answering this way, prefer another instance.

window.truncated_note: At least one instance had more orders than it could return in one page, so the comparison was limited to the range where both are known to be complete. {excluded} orders fell outside that range and could not be checked either way.

error.identity_mismatch: Couldn't sign — your account session looks out of sync. Sign out, then sign back in to fix this.

download.title: Get {brand}
download.subtitle: Install {brand} as an app on any device, or get the source code. No app store, no gatekeeper — and the code is mirrored across the web so it can't be taken down.
download.operator_section_subtitle: Anyone can run a Morphit node — your own brand, your own users, your own fee revenue. The federation finds you automatically. Below is everything you need.
download.operator_source_body: Morphit is AGPL-3.0. Clone the repo, run the smoke suite, deploy. Each release is signed and its SHA-256 manifest is published on the blockchain so you can verify what you cloned matches what the project published.
download.operator_verify_note: Every release artifact (source tarball and offline bundle) has its SHA-256 hash recorded on the blockchain in a `morphit_release_v1` op signed by @morphit. Verify a download by re-hashing it locally and comparing against that signed record — scripts/verify-download.mjs does both, asking two Blurt nodes on different hosts and checking the signature.
download.operator_setup_body: We don't ship pre-built `.deb` or `.rpm` packages — Morphit is a multi-component server (Postgres + Node.js indexer + relay + reverse proxy) and one-package installs would hide the architecture from you. Instead, the operator handbook walks you through it step-by-step.
download.operator_setup_doc_ops: OPERATIONS.md — ongoing operator runbook (backups, top-ups, RPC management)
download.operator_setup_doc_switching: SWITCHING-NETWORKS.md — staging procedure + going-live launch checklist
download.operator_distros_body: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS is the best-tested choice, and the one-command installer also accepts its derivatives — it reads the Ubuntu 'noble' base, so the edition doesn't matter: Linux Mint 22, Pop!_OS, Zorin OS 17, KDE neon, and elementary OS all work. Debian 12+ and hardened-Debian bases like Kicksecure work via the manual setup steps — both make excellent lean, security-focused servers. Any modern Linux with Node.js 22+ and Postgres 15+ should run it (Arch, Alpine, NixOS — you're more on your own there); FreeBSD works with minor adjustments. Hardware: any 2-core ARM64 or x86-64 machine with 4 GB RAM and 80 GB SSD — most operators run on a Raspberry Pi 4, an Intel mini-PC, or a spare laptop.
download.operator_join_body: Once your instance is live and broadcasting `morphit_operator_register_v1`, it appears in every other Morphit instance's directory automatically. No application, no permission, no central listing.
download.pwa_body: {brand} installs straight from your browser as an app — on Android, iPhone, iPad, and desktop. There's no app store, no sign-up, and no gatekeeper who can pull it. Once installed it works offline and updates itself. We don't build native APK / iOS / Flatpak packages — the PWA covers every platform.
download.pwa_platforms: Android (Chrome, Brave…): open the browser menu and choose “Install app” or “Add to Home screen”. iPhone & iPad (Safari): tap Share, then “Add to Home Screen”. Desktop (Chrome, Edge, Brave): click the install icon in the address bar.
download.mirrors_body: Morphit is fully open source (AGPL-3.0). The canonical repository lives on our own Forgejo server and is mirrored across the web, so the code stays reachable even if one host is blocked or disappears.
download.ipns_note: The IPNS link resolves the latest release peer-to-peer, with no DNS and no third party — it needs an IPFS-capable browser (like Brave) or a local IPFS node. In any other browser, the IPFS link works everywhere. You can also copy the permanent address into your own node:

why_agpl.q: Why does Morphit use the AGPL-3.0 license?
why_agpl.a:
So that no one — not a corporation, not a government, not even us — can take Morphit, lock it up, and quietly turn it against the people using it. The license guarantees that every running copy of Morphit stays open and inspectable. Everything else here is built on that.

**The one rule it adds.** If you run Morphit as a public service and you change the code, you have to share your changes with the people using it. That's the whole deal. Run an instance, rebrand it, rewrite every word on the screen, add features, charge for it — all fine, and encouraged. The only thing you can't do is run a *secret, modified* version. If your instance can reach users, your users can read its source. For a privacy tool that's the whole game: it's how anyone can confirm the instance they're on is the real Morphit and not a backdoored look-alike. Freedom you can't verify is just a promise — this turns it into something you can check.

**Why not a "freer" license?** Permissive licenses (MIT, BSD, Apache) ask for nothing in return, which sounds freer — until you notice it also lets anyone take Morphit, bolt on hidden tracking, close the source, and sell it back to your neighbors as a polished surveillance app, with no one the wiser. A license that permits your own capture isn't protecting your freedom; it's protecting whoever wants to cage you. The plain GPL has the same hole for network software: it only triggers when you hand someone a program to download, not when you run a modified copy on your own server — which is exactly how people use Morphit. The AGPL closes that hole. And no license at all is the worst of the lot: say nothing, and copyright law defaults to *all rights reserved* — no one may legally fork it or run their own instance. Silence isn't freedom; it's a locked door.

**For agorists especially.** Here's the honest tension: the AGPL leans on copyright, and copyright is a creature of the State. The purist position is to claim nothing — drop it into the public domain and walk away. We think that hands a gift to the exact people you're trying to escape: the well-funded actors who'll take it, close it, wire it into the surveillance machine, and call it convenient. Pure intentions, captured tool. Copyleft is the judo move — it takes the State's own instrument and turns it against enclosure. We're not begging the State for protection; we're using its own rules to make this commons permanently un-takeable. Every fork stays open. Every instance stays inspectable. Nobody gets to build a cage out of our code. That's not making peace with the system — it's the system finally working for the counter-economy instead of against it.

**The bigger picture.** The point was never to win an argument with the beast — it's to make it obsolete. The more people who run their own instances, and talk others into running even more, the less there is for any central power to control: tools it can't surveil, markets it can't see, exchange it can't tax or stop. That's what renders the apparatus pointless. It won't be graceful — when control slips, the first reflex is always to grab harder, with more rules and more force. But coercion is expensive and futility is exhausting, and sooner or later the beast does what bullies do once no one's afraid: it loses interest and goes off to find something more productive to do. So fork Morphit. Make it yours. Stand up an instance, and talk three friends into standing up three more. The license is here to guarantee one thing — that every one of those instances stays free, open, and impossible to quietly turn against the people who use it.

*Morphit is released under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3. This is our reasoning, not legal advice.*

what_is_morphit.a: Morphit is a P2P marketplace where people trade cash for cryptocurrency (Bitcoin, Monero, Blurt, USDT, USD Coin (USDC), Dai, Bitcoin Cash, Litecoin, Dash, Dogecoin, Zcash, Pirate Chain, Decred, Solana, Ethereum, and XRP) directly with each other. Barter goods/services too. Morphit never touches your assets and never asks anything about you. It's a decentralised/distributed bulletin board service (DBBS), not a bank.

is_it_safe.a:
Much safer than platforms that hold your funds — because {brand} can't lose or freeze what it never had. The real risk is your trading partner, so always check their reputation score before agreeing to trade.

Reputation is everything; even when the only thing that {brand} "knows" about them is that their name is @scooby. If you want to build your reputation around the name @dingleberry, go for it. {brand} shows the completed trades, feedback, and how long a user has been around.

vs_others.q: How is Morphit different from LocalBitcoins or LocalMonero?
vs_others.a:
Short version: Morphit goes further on decentralization, privacy, and non-custody than either of them — and deliberately does less in exchange.

LocalBitcoins (RIP, 2023) and LocalMonero (closed 2024) were centralized companies with custodial escrow. When a trade went wrong, their human arbitrators held the coins and decided who got them. When the companies shut down — by regulator pressure or business decision — their entire user base, reputations, dispute history, and ongoing trades vanished overnight. Morphit cannot be shut down in the same way: there are no central arbitrators, no custodial wallets, no company bank account to freeze. Every order lives on-chain, every trade is peer-to-peer, and anyone can run an indexer or frontend. Multiple instances on four networks (clearnet, Tor, Lokinet, I2P) mean blocking one node does nothing.

On privacy: Morphit pushes harder than either of them on transport, storage, and chat.
• Transport: four parallel networks, all first-class (not just an 'onion mode').
• Storage: nothing about you lives on Morphit's servers — keys are in your browser, orders are on-chain, chats are on-chain as ciphertext only. You can move to any device with just your 12-word seed.
• Chat: end-to-end encrypted using X25519 key agreement plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 (from libsodium), with a per-message ephemeral key. LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero chats were visible to staff. Morphit chat is encrypted on your device, stored as ciphertext on the blockchain, and decryptable only by the two participants — operators and chain observers see nothing. We deliberately chose a simple, fast, low-bundle-weight ECIES design.

On non-custody: LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero held your coins during a trade. Morphit never touches them at any point, period — the seller sends directly to the buyer when payment is confirmed. That is more trust placed on reputation, less on cryptography; honest about the tradeoff.

On arbitration: LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero arbitrators could overrule feedback. Morphit has no arbitrator role at all; feedback is permanent and signed on chain. If you scam someone, your public key carries that feedback forever; you cannot appeal to a human. That's a strong disincentive for repeat scammers and zero protection for first-time ones — hence the emphasis on checking account age and reputation.

What Morphit doesn't have that they did: escrow, human arbitration, per-market moderation. **Morphit will never offer any of these.** Reintroducing escrow, multisig, or arbitration would reintroduce the middleman this project exists to remove. Morphit's advantage is that it's lean, portable, browser-native, fully decentralized at every layer, and impossible to shut down — and its tradeoff is that you trade on immutable, provable reputation.

vs_atomic_swap_dexes.q: How is Morphit different from BasicSwap?
vs_atomic_swap_dexes.a:
BasicSwap is a kindred project in the no-middleman peer-to-peer space, but it makes different architectural choices than Morphit. It does cross-chain atomic swaps directly between two wallets — no escrow, no arbitrator, no central server. We're aligned on the principle; the tradeoffs differ.

• **You have to install it first.** BasicSwap is a desktop app or Docker setup: you install and run it before you can even browse the orderbook. Morphit's orderbook is a public web page on any instance, browsable from any phone without installing anything.

• **It runs full nodes.** BasicSwap typically runs a full node for every chain it trades — Bitcoin, Monero, Litecoin. First sync takes hours to days, and storage, CPU and bandwidth costs continue. Morphit is a browser tab.

• **Swaps are slow, and both parties must stay online.** A cross-chain atomic swap needs confirmations on both chains; a BTC ↔ XMR swap typically locks coins for 30 minutes to several hours. Both wallets must be live for the whole multi-step exchange — if your counterparty disappears mid-swap, you wait out the refund timelock to get your coins back. Morphit trades need no simultaneous presence: you post an order, the other party acts when they're ready. Coordination finalizes on the next block, about 3 seconds. (Settlement of the underlying asset still takes whatever the chosen chain or payment method takes — Morphit doesn't claim otherwise.)

• **Crypto-only, no fiat.** BasicSwap trades crypto for crypto. Morphit also does fiat ↔ crypto in whatever payment method two people agree on — bank transfer, cash, gift card, in-game currency — plus barter (gold bars, banana trees, whatever).

• **No reputation, no chat.** BasicSwap has no network-wide feedback system and no messaging layer; negotiation happens somewhere else. Morphit feedback is signed on-chain and follows your public key across every instance, and chat is end-to-end encrypted on your device, stored as ciphertext on the chain.

**On the July 2026 exploit.** BasicSwap was exploited on 14 July 2026, with confirmed losses of more than 0.66 BTC (about $42,000 at the time), reported by the project's own developer @ofrnxmr and by Orangefren. We mention it because anyone choosing between two ways to trade should know it happened — not to score a point. Atomic swaps are still a beautiful piece of cryptographic engineering, and the idea is not what broke. Morphit has no room to gloat here either: we are software, we have bugs, and the honest difference is architectural rather than moral. Morphit never takes custody of your coins, so there is no pot for an attacker to drain — but a bug in our code could still cost you a trade, and we would rather say so plainly than pretend otherwise.

Both designs are valid. They serve different users.

vs_bisq_haveno.q: How is Morphit different from Bisq or Haveno/Retoswap?
vs_bisq_haveno.a:
Bisq and Haveno (and Haveno's fork Retoswap) are the closest projects to Morphit in spirit — non-custodial, peer-to-peer, no KYC. Haveno is itself a fork of Bisq, so the two share the same underlying design; here's how each compares to Morphit.

**Bisq** is a long-running peer-to-peer marketplace with the same architectural pattern as Haveno: desktop Java application, 2-of-3 multisig escrow during trades, Tor for transport, arbitrated disputes when something goes wrong. Bisq has been compromised twice with user funds stolen — the kind of risk Morphit avoids by never touching user funds in the first place. Bisq also requires you to lock up BSQ collateral before you can list orders. Morphit locks up nothing from anyone.

Haveno (and its fork Retoswap) is much closer in spirit — non-custodial, P2P, no KYC. The big differences: Haveno is a desktop-only Java/JavaFX application tied to the Monero blockchain for its 2-of-3 multisig escrow, and needs you to run (or connect to) a seednode. Morphit runs in any browser, on any phone, with no install; uses Blurt (not Monero) for its on-chain coordination layer, which is faster and far cheaper per action (~free vs. Monero's per-op fees); and ships with built-in Tor, Lokinet, and I2P reachability rather than relying on you to configure it. Haveno trades involve arbitrated escrow, which is strong but requires trusted arbitrators per market. Morphit v1 is pure reputation-based bulletin board — no escrow, no arbitrator, full responsibility on the traders to pick partners with real track records. That's a more conservative safety model, but also fewer centralized choke points and no arbitrator role that a government could pressure.

On May 20, 2026 the Haveno trade protocol was exploited for approximately $2.7 million. The attack used a forged out-of-order acknowledgment message from a fake arbitrator to redirect the 2-of-3 multisig wallet address before user funds were deposited; RetoSwap halted trading the same day. Morphit's design has no arbitrator role, no multisig escrow, and no central coordination message Haveno's exploit relied on — so this attack class doesn't apply to our threat model. The tradeoff is real and stated above: Morphit users carry full self-custody and lean on signed on-chain reputation rather than an arbitrator's safety net.

Then, on June 16, 2026, the Haveno protocol was exploited a second time in under a month — this time through its dispute-resolution and forced-arbitration path. An attacker posing as a buyer forced a dispute and had the seller's XMR released after the Bitcoin side showed its confirmations, without ever actually sending the BTC; early tracking by orangefren put the loss around 1,500 XMR (roughly $500,000), and RetoSwap again suspended trading and raised the minimum client version. Two protocol-level exploits in under thirty days — both in the arbitration and dispute machinery — are the clearest illustration of the tradeoff above: an arbitrator-and-escrow safety net is also an attack surface. Morphit has no arbitrator, no forced-arbitration step, no dispute payout, and no multisig escrow — so neither the May acknowledgment-spoofing attack nor the June dispute-forgery attack has anything to target in our model.

vs_openmonero.q: How is Morphit different from OpenMonero?
vs_openmonero.a:
OpenMonero (a LocalMonero clone) is a custodial platform, and it has lost user funds more than once. On June 6, 2025, a misconfigured firewall and wallet-rpc combination drained roughly 77.85 XMR (about $25,225) from the platform's internal custodial wallet; OpenMonero says it has since refunded affected users out of trading fees, a process that ran for about a year, with vendors prioritized. On May 21, 2026 — one day after the first Haveno exploit — OpenMonero posted a fresh exploit alert and told users to halt all payments while it investigated. Morphit has no custodial wallet at all; your XMR never sits on a Morphit server, so this entire attack class has nothing to steal. The pattern across the sector is consistent: platforms that hold user funds in an internal wallet tend to get drained eventually. Morphit's answer is to not hold them in the first place.

OpenMonero went offline briefly in early June 2026 and then returned later that month, saying it is more secure "this time" and pointing to new server-side hardening such as runtime encryption, hardened deployments, and memory encryption. That kind of hardening protects OpenMonero's own custodial wallet and servers — but it doesn't change the fact that there is a custodial wallet there to protect, and to lose. Morphit's difference is structural, not a matter of degree: there is no Morphit wallet, so there is nothing to harden, nothing to drain, and no operator who could quietly go offline holding your coins. The seller sends XMR straight to the buyer once payment is confirmed, and Morphit never touches it. Morphit is also fully open source with zero code obfuscation — every line that runs in your browser is published and auditable — whereas OpenMonero obfuscates parts of its code, so you cannot fully check what it does with your funds.

video_tutorial.a: Yes — we host short video tutorials on Blurt.media, a decentralized PeerTube/Peerhub instance, also syndicated to the Fediverse and multiple networks. Watch at https://blurt.media (search for "Morphit"). We link out rather than embed because video embeds come with trade-offs for privacy: a PeerTube iframe would expose your IP to other viewers in the P2P swarm. Opening Blurt.media in a new tab keeps you in control. If you use a VPN or Tor Browser (recommended), your IP is already protected and the embed trade-off disappears.

signup_requirements.q: What do I need to sign up?
signup_requirements.a: Nothing. No email, no phone number, no name. Your browser generates a cryptographic keypair on your device — that is your entire account. Write down the 12-word recovery seed and you're done.

how_to_buy.a: Open the orderbook and Filter it by the cryptocurrency that you want. Pick a seller with a good reputation, click the Message button to respond to their post and in the chat you two agree on the details. You then pay the seller at least the minimum value amount (cash, crypto, bank transfer, barter, etc) as per your agreement. You provably send the funds (or complete the barter agreement) and then the crypto seller sends the crypto directly to your crypto wallet. Leave each other a Feedback review and you're done!

how_to_sell.a: Post an order listing what you're selling — any of the assets {brand} supports (BTC, XMR, BLURT, stablecoins and more) — where you are, and which payment methods you accept. A buyer will open a chat with you to agree on details. When you confirm you received their payment, you send them the crypto (or whatever you agreed to exchange). Leave honest feedback when done — it helps everyone.

fees.a:
Three things to know:

1. {brand} never takes a cut of your trade itself. The price you and your counterparty agree on is the price you receive — nothing is skimmed. {brand} isn't an escrow and doesn't touch your funds.

2. Posting an order costs a small network fee:
 • **$0.25 USD-equivalent** if you pay in BTC or XMR (full price)
 • **$0.125 USD-equivalent** if you pay in Blurt (a deliberate 50% discount)
 The discount exists because Morphit's coordination layer runs on Blurt's blockchain with 3-second confirmation times. Paying in Blurt is the default option, costs half as much, and counts toward loyalty-milestone Blurt Power (BP) rewards (see "How loyalty rewards work"). The compose screen shows the exact amount in your chosen currency before you sign — no surprises.

3. Your very first buy order is free. We waive the network fee on your first-ever buy — a small welcome gift so new traders can try {brand} risk-free. See "Is my first order really free?" for the details.

There's also an optional "featured" slot you can bid on if you want your order to stand out — a per-hour cost that you only pay if you actively want the visibility.

A note on the spam-deterrent escalation: post a lot of orders quickly (4+ in a 24-hour window) and the per-order fee starts climbing. This is the anti-Sybil tier — it bites spammers far more than real users, who rarely post more than 2-3 listings in a day. The compose screen shows you the current tier multiplier before you sign so there's no surprise. The Sybil escalation only applies to Blurt-paid orders; BTC and XMR fees are flat at the base rate.

trade_goods_services.q: Can I trade goods or services on {brand}, like fruit trees or vintage records?
trade_goods_services.a:
**Yes — and for some people, this is the whole point of Morphit.** If you're unbanked, living under capital controls, or watching your national currency lose value by the week, being able to turn your goods and your labor directly into hard money — without asking a bank's permission — isn't a convenience, it's a lifeline. That's counter-economics in practice: ordinary people anonymously trading peer-to-peer in a free market, outside the gatekeepers. Morphit is built for exactly this.

How it works: **every Morphit order has a tradable coin on one side (BTC, XMR, Blurt, or any asset {brand} lists), and whatever you agree on for the other side** — a national currency, a different coin, or **goods and services.** To trade goods or services, choose the `Barter (goods/services)` payment method and describe the deal in the `terms` field.

*Example 1 — selling orange trees for Monero:* Go to the Post page, then click on `I want to BUY`. Select Monero (XMR). Select which fiat currency you would normally sell those trees for such as Pesos, Euros, Dollars, etc. Select the `Barter (goods/services)` payment method. Set your Terms, for example: `"$20 per orange tree at least 1-2m tall. Pick them up at my farm (or advise me on your location address for shipment ($5 more per tree))."` Anyone holding XMR who wants your trees can accept your offer.

*Example 2 — selling your mobile car wash service for Monero:* Same process, but in the Terms field you might say something like this: `"I'll come to your business and wash your car. I charge $30 per car. Dry and wax for an additional $20. See my ad in the local newspaper! Wash Boy, Inc."`

**The one rule:** one side must be a coin that {brand} supports. That's what gives every trade a real, on-chain receipt and lets honest traders build a reputation that travels with them — the trust a free market runs on.

cash_by_mail_walkthrough.q: How do I trade cash by mail or ship physical goods through {brand}?
cash_by_mail_walkthrough.a:
Cash-by-mail and shipped-goods trades work like any other {brand} trade, with two extra chat tools:

**1. Mailing-address share.** In the chat composer, tap **"Share mailing address"**. The form has fields for country, street, city, postal/ZIP code, optional state/province, optional recipient name, optional second line (apt/suite), and an optional note. Your address stays end-to-end encrypted in chat — only you and your trade partner can read it. Like every chat message it travels as ciphertext: the encrypted form is stored permanently on the Blurt chain and by indexers, and nobody but the two of you can decrypt it — unless one of your chat keys leaks later. The privacy aside in the modal reminds you that sharing is irreversible (once sent, your partner has it even if you clear the message later) and suggests using a P.O. box, mail-drop service, or virtual mailbox if you don't want to share your home address.

**2. Shipment record.** After you mail the cash or the goods, tap **"Record shipment"** in the chat composer. Pick a carrier from the dropdown (USPS, UPS, FedEx, DHL Express, Royal Mail, La Poste, Deutsche Post, Poste Italiane, Correos, Poczta Polska, Pochta Rossii, China Post EMS, Hongkong Post, Japan Post, Australia Post, Canada Post, India Post, Iran Post, SF Express, Aramex, or **Other** with a free-text name + tracking URL), enter the tracking number from your receipt, and optionally add a note ("Shipped today, ETA Friday"). Your partner sees a **📦 Shipped via X** pill in chat with a clickable "Track package" link. Tracking number is optional — submit without if you used untracked mail — but recommended as proof of shipment.

**Safety tips for any physical shipment** (shown in the modal aside):

- Use a tracked, **insured** service. If the package is lost or stolen, insurance is your only recourse.
- Use a **plain envelope or box** with no markings suggesting valuables inside.
- **Return address tradeoff**: omitting your return address preserves anonymity but means undeliverable mail gets destroyed. There's no right answer; pick based on your threat model.
- Tracking number is optional but strongly recommended.

**If you're mailing CASH** (collapsible expander in the modal):

- **Wrap the cash in aluminum foil inside the envelope.** This defeats people holding envelopes up to bright light to see contents — a well-known soft attack on mailed paper currency.
- **UPS and FedEx PROHIBIT cash shipments in their terms of service.** If they open the package, they can confiscate it with no recourse. Use a postal service instead (USPS, Royal Mail, Deutsche Post, La Poste, etc.).
- **International**: don't lie on customs declarations. High-value cash will be seized regardless of how it's declared.

**For sellers receiving tracking numbers — sanity-check spoofing.** A scammy buyer could paste any random tracking number. Before you ship crypto, look up the tracking number on the carrier's site (📋 Copy the number from the pill, then paste into the carrier's tracker via your normal browser or Tor) and **verify the destination ZIP code matches your actual ZIP**. If a number resolves to a package being delivered to someone else's city, the buyer is trying to scam you.

**ELI5 for grandma:**

You want to buy some Monero (a digital currency) from somebody on {brand}. The seller wants U.S. dollars cash, sent through the mail. Here's what happens:

1. The seller's order says "Selling 0.05 XMR for $100 USD via Cash by mail."
2. You take the order. A chat opens.
3. The seller taps "Share mailing address" and fills in their P.O. box. You see a 📬 pill with the address. You tap "Copy address" to copy it.
4. You go to the post office. You wrap five $20 bills in tinfoil, put them in a plain envelope addressed to that P.O. box, buy USPS Priority Mail with insurance, and write down the tracking number from your receipt.
5. Back in {brand} chat, you tap "Record shipment", pick USPS, paste the tracking number, and send.
6. The seller sees a 📦 pill with your tracking number and clicks "Track package" to verify on the USPS site that the destination ZIP matches their P.O. box's ZIP.
7. A few days later, the package arrives. The seller picks it up, opens it, counts the cash, and then sends the 0.05 XMR to your Monero wallet (via {brand}'s existing "Share address" + "Mark as sent" flow).
8. You leave each other positive feedback. Done.

**Limitations.** {brand} does not arbitrate disputes. If your cash gets lost in the mail and you didn't use insurance, that's between you and the carrier — {brand} cannot recover it. If the seller takes your cash and never sends the crypto, file a feedback report and the community sees their reputation drop, but {brand} cannot reverse the cash transfer. The same is true for any P2P platform that doesn't custody funds. Insurance + verified addresses + good carrier choice + small first trades to build trust are your real protections.

order_timeouts.q: How long do orders stay open?
order_timeouts.a: Orders stay visible for up to 90 days by default (you can change this 1–90 days). You have 15 minutes after posting to replace an order for typos; after that it's locked. Trades themselves happen off-platform — Morphit coordinates the order match, but you and your counterparty agree on the payment timeline directly via the encrypted chat. Most pairs settle within hours; long-running disputes are rare because feedback discipline incentivizes both sides to close out quickly. If your order expires without a match, you can re-list it from /my/orders with one click.

order_editing.q: Can I fix or cancel an order after posting?
order_editing.a: You have 15 minutes after posting to replace an order (for typos or wrong numbers). After 15 minutes, or as soon as someone expresses interest in trading, the order is locked. You can still cancel it — cancellation is its own on-chain action, always allowed before a trade begins. Technically: Blurt's `custom_json` ops are permanent and not editable at the protocol level, so Morphit handles 'edits' by posting a tiny replacement op that references the original. Both versions live on chain forever — anyone can audit the full history — but indexers only accept replacements posted within the 15-minute window. Why 15 minutes? A longer window is an attack: a seller could post favorable terms, wait for a buyer to start negotiating, then silently worsen them. Fifteen minutes is enough to catch a typo during proofreading, short enough that no real conversation has started.

chat_privacy.a:
Your chat content is private — encrypted end-to-end between you and your counterparty. Only your two devices hold the keys to decrypt.

What's private:
• Message text
• Any payment details, addresses, or negotiation you exchange

What's not private (visible to anyone reading the chain):
• Who you chat with, and when each message was sent
• Which order a conversation is about (the order's id travels in clear text with each message)
• Approximate message size
• Read receipts: when you open a conversation, your browser publishes up to what time you have read it
• Whom you block

Cryptography used:
• X25519 key agreement: a fresh one-time key per message, combined with both parties' chat keys, so a message also proves to the recipient who sent it
• ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption
• BLAKE2b key derivation

These are standard primitives from libsodium; the design is documented in ADR-0015 and docs/CHAT-CRYPTO.md. There is no forward secrecy: anyone who later obtains the recipient's chat key can read every message sent to them. If your threat model needs that, use a dedicated secure messenger — good options include **Matrix/Element**, **Session** and **Signal**. (Morphit complements but doesn't replace a dedicated secure messenger.)

monero_amount_jitter.q: Why does Morphit randomize my transfer amount?
monero_amount_jitter.a:
Identical amounts on a public chain are a fingerprint. If you post an order to sell 0.00513924 BTC and the buyer sends you exactly 0.00513924 BTC, an observer watching the chain — your ISP-attached forensic team, a chain-analysis firm, a curious neighbor running an indexer — can match the chain transfer to your orderbook post with high confidence. Morphit defeats this by adding a tiny random tail to every transfer so the on-chain amount differs from the posted amount by a small unpredictable number. The seller is always paid slightly MORE than asked, never less; verification still passes because the amount-check is 'at-least.'

**Why this matters even on 'transparent' chains you chose deliberately.** Choosing Bitcoin (or BCH, LTC, DASH, DOGE, transparent ZEC, SOL, ETH, XRP, etc.) doesn't mean you've consented to having every trade publicly linked to your username. The point of using a transparent chain is auditability of supply and infrastructure trust — not surveillance of your individual trades. Jitter shrinks the linkability without changing anything else about your trade. Think of it like wearing a hat in a parade: you're still in public, you've just removed the bit of identifying detail that wasn't required to be there.

**Why this matters even on Monero.** Monero hides amounts on chain — but the amount you SHARE in the chat goes through other surfaces. Centralized exchanges you off-ramp to see the figure. Counterparties you message see the figure. Screenshots leak. Wallet histories on your device record the figure. If chat-shared amounts and on-chain transfers can be linked by an observer who learns just one of them, the privacy advantage of XMR weakens. Jitter restores that gap.

**Per-asset jitter range** (all under a cent in most cases):
- **XMR**: up to 999,999 piconero (~$0.0002)
- **BTC / BCH / LTC / DASH / DOGE / ZEC / ARRR / DCR / SOL / ETH / XRP**: up to 999 satoshi-equivalents (~$0.001 to $0.50 depending on price)
- **Blurt**: up to 99 milliblurt (fractions of a cent)
- **USDT / USDC / DAI**: up to 999 micro-units (under a tenth of a cent)

**Default ON.** The toggle sits right under the amount field in the address-share modal. We strongly recommend you leave it on — the cost is a trivial implicit tip, the privacy benefit is meaningful. Turning it off should be a deliberate informed choice (for example, when matching an exact invoice amount that a counterparty's accounting system requires).

**What jitter does NOT do.** It addresses amount-correlation linkability, not the separate centralization threat that USDT/USDC/DAI carry (Circle/Tether can freeze addresses regardless of amount). For full per-asset privacy posture see /privacy/{asset}.

feedback_immutable.q: Can feedback be edited or deleted?
feedback_immutable.a:
No, once posted it is permanent. This is what makes reputation meaningful — nobody can quietly erase a bad review. If someone leaves feedback you disagree with, you can post a public response; the original stays.

**If people are going to trust you, your reputation is everything.**

data_collection.q: What data does Morphit collect about me?
data_collection.a: Very little, and none of it is about who you are. No cookies, no analytics, no tracking scripts, no telemetry, no email, no phone number, no ID. Your IP address reaches the server like with any website; Morphit's code keeps it only in memory for rate limiting (at most 24 hours, for the signup limits) and never writes it down. What you publish yourself — orders, reviews, and the encrypted chat messages with their sender, recipient and time — is on the public Blurt chain. If you turn on push notifications, the instance's relay stores your account name with the push address your browser's vendor gave you, until you turn them off. The full list is in the repository's docs/METADATA-LEAK-CATALOG.md.

lost_keys.q: What if I lose my password or recovery seed?
lost_keys.a:
Your account is inaccessible, and we cannot get it back for you. This is not a mistake — it's the core design. If there were any recovery mechanism, someone would have access to your keys. We refuse to be that someone. Secure those 12-words like your life depends on it.

The same is true if you signed in with an existing Blurt account: your Keyfile and your keys are the account. Lose both and no one — not us, not the operator, not the blockchain — can restore them.

what_is_blurt.q: Why did Morphit choose the Blurt blockchain?
what_is_blurt.a:
We needed a public **social** blockchain — and that constraint eliminated almost everything else on the market.

Privacy-focused chains like Monero (which we love and trade as a primary asset) are built around hiding amounts, addresses, and metadata. Their users — rightly — refuse to broadcast structured public data because that's antithetical to the whole reason those chains exist. You can't run a public orderbook, immutable reputation system, or auditable trade history on a surveillance-resistant chain; the surveillance resistance is the whole point.

But Morphit's coordination layer needs the opposite: orders, prices, feedback, and order announcements that ANYONE can read and verify, without trusting Morphit. So we needed a chain explicitly designed for public structured data — a SOCIAL chain. After auditing the field (Hive, Steem, Blurt, Lens, Farcaster, ATProto), Blurt won on every metric that mattered:

**1. Three-second block times.** Real-time orderbook updates. New orders confirm in seconds, not minutes — fast enough that high-frequency traders can place and accept orders without lag, and fast enough to **prevent eBay-style last-second sniping**. There's no time window where someone can rush in and grab an order ahead of a buyer who saw it first.

**2. Throughput exceeding Visa + Mastercard combined.** Blurt's witness network can process more transactions per second than every major card network put together. Morphit will never compete with Blurt social-content posts for chain capacity. Listing fees stay tiny because there's no congestion.

**3. Transactions are essentially free.** No mining. No gas auctions. No priority-fee arms races. Posting an order, broadcasting feedback, sending an encrypted chat message — these cost effectively zero in chain fees. Morphit's $0.125 listing fee isn't a chain cost; it's a project decision (anti-Sybil + cover account-creation costs). On a chain like Ethereum or Bitcoin, the fees alone would make a $5 trade impossible.

**4. Built-in end-to-end encrypted chat.** Buyer–seller conversations live on chain as encrypted ciphertexts. Permanent, verifiable, decentralized — and only the two parties hold the keys to read them. Trade-coordination history is durable for posterity (and for any future dispute, you have a courtroom-grade record).
