privacy.index_intro: Most assets traded on {brand} (BTC, BCH, LTC, DASH, DOGE, DCR, SOL, ETH, XRP, BLURT, USDT, USDC, DAI) live on transparent chains — any observer can read the chain history. Zcash (ZEC) is transparent unless you use its shielded addresses; Pirate Chain (ARRR), like Monero, hides sender, receiver and amount by default. There are concrete steps you can take to make YOUR trades much harder to link, profile, or surveil. This is registry-driven: the next asset Morphit adds will get a guide automatically. Beyond individual trades, Morphit also protects privacy at the network level: it can be reached and run entirely over Tor and I2P — a node can even operate with zero clearnet at all — as detailed on the Security page and the instance directory.
privacy.section_fresh_addresses: Use a fresh address every trade
privacy.section_opt_in_tech_intro: Standards that wallets in this ecosystem may implement. {brand} does NOT recommend specific wallet software — even reputable wallets have been compromised. Search for a wallet that supports these standards and review its trust posture yourself.
privacy.no_wallet_recommendation: {brand} does NOT recommend specific wallet software. Even reputable wallets have been compromised or have had hidden flaws. The privacy techniques here are protocol standards, not endorsements — your wallet, your responsibility.

fresh_address_advice.subaddress: This chain supports stealth/subaddress technology natively. Your wallet derives a fresh receive address (subaddress) per trade from your view key. The recipient sees a unique address every time; chain observers cannot link multiple trades to the same wallet.
fresh_address_advice.hd-derived: This chain uses transparent addresses with no native stealth. The standard practice: use a Hierarchical Deterministic (BIP-32) wallet that derives a new receive address per request. Most modern wallets do this automatically. The cost of address reuse is severe — every trade you accept at the same address builds a public record of your activity.
fresh_address_advice.account-reuse: This chain is account-based — your account name is your address. Fresh-account-per-trade is not practical (each new account costs chain resources). Accept that this asset has the highest amount-correlation risk on {brand}. For high-value trades, consider using an alt-account dedicated to that trade.

mweb.name: MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks)
mweb.explain: A native Litecoin protocol-level privacy feature. MWEB hides transaction amounts and breaks the address-to-amount link for transfers that opt in. Per-transaction; not chain-wide. Look for wallets that surface "MWEB" or "Extension Blocks" as an option when sending.

cashfusion.name: CashFusion
cashfusion.explain: A Bitcoin Cash CoinJoin variant designed by the BCH community. Mixes inputs and outputs of varying amounts to defeat both common-input-ownership and amount-correlation heuristics. Run from a wallet that supports CashFusion before or after a trade to launder the on-chain history.

coinjoin.name: CoinJoin
coinjoin.explain: A family of protocols where multiple participants pool inputs and outputs into a single transaction, breaking the common-input-ownership heuristic that links coins to one owner. Multiple implementations exist with different trust models — choose carefully and read the implementation's threat model.

payjoin.name: PayJoin (BIP-78)
payjoin.explain: A two-party cooperative transaction protocol. Sender and receiver both contribute inputs, so chain observers cannot apply the standard "all inputs come from the same wallet" heuristic. {brand}'s address-share modal includes an optional PayJoin endpoint field — if both wallets support BIP-78, the trade automatically uses PayJoin.

privatesend.name: PrivateSend
privatesend.explain: Dash's native CoinJoin variant. Uses denominated input/output amounts and masternode coordination to mix coins among multiple participants, breaking the link between sender and receiver on-chain. Run multiple mixing rounds (more rounds = larger anonymity set = higher fee). Pre-mix in your Dash wallet BEFORE sharing the address — by the time the funds reach {brand} they're already mixed.

shielded-pools.name: Shielded pools (Sapling + Orchard)
shielded-pools.explain: Zcash's protocol-level privacy. Shielded transactions (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address) use zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Sapling is the established shielded pool (since 2018); Orchard is the newer pool (Network Upgrade 5, 2022) accessed through Unified Addresses. Per-address — recipients pick z/u-addr for shielded transactions or t-addr for transparent. Both transparent and shielded are first-class on the protocol. Wallets that fully support shielded sends: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk Wallet (mobile, Sapling). Older wallets may only support transparent (t-addr) sends, so confirm your counterparty's wallet supports the address type you intend to use.

csppmix.name: CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing
csppmix.explain: A wallet-side mixing protocol that bundles your transaction inputs with other participants in a single multi-party round.  After mixing, your outputs are no longer linkable to your original inputs on chain.  Integrated into dcrwallet for Decred — enable the "Mix Account" option.  Opt-in (you choose when to mix); off-protocol (mixing rounds aren't enforced by consensus).

common_practices.fresh_per_trade: **Use a fresh receive address for every trade.** Your wallet should support this; if it doesn't, look for one that does. Address reuse is the single biggest leak.
common_practices.coin_control: **Practice coin control when spending.** When sending coins later, avoid combining the trade output with coins from another source — that combines their address histories permanently.
common_practices.network_layer: **Broadcast through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode.** Your home IP address sees the transaction first; nodes near your IP can correlate it to you. A Tor-aware wallet broadcasts through Tor by default.
common_practices.kyc_touchpoints: **Avoid sending trade coins to or from KYC exchanges.** Once trade coins touch a KYC exchange, the trade becomes legally identifiable by combining exchange records with chain data. If you need to bridge to fiat, route through a self-custodied intermediate step.

what_not_to_do.reuse_address: Do not paste your same receive address into multiple trades.
what_not_to_do.exact_amount: Do not send the exact amount listed on the order — {brand}'s amount-randomizer toggle (the "🔐 Randomize amount" checkbox in the address-share modal) breaks this; leave it ON.
what_not_to_do.combine_utxos: Do not combine the trade output with coins from a different source when you later spend it.
what_not_to_do.clearnet_broadcast: Do not broadcast from your home IP via a non-private wallet — use Tor.

btc.one_line: Transparent chain, fully decentralized — opt-in mixing protocols available.
btc.intro: Bitcoin is the most-analyzed chain in the world. Every transaction is public; every address can be tracked over time. The privacy practices below dramatically reduce how easily a third party can profile your trades — without requiring you to leave BTC.
btc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, PayJoin, CoinJoin, and what to avoid.

xmr.one_line: Privacy by default — stealth addresses, hidden amounts, ring signatures.
xmr.intro: Monero's chain-level privacy hides sender, recipient, and amount by default. By default, your address, amount, and counterparty are hidden from third parties. The practices below are minor tightenings; the chain itself does the heavy lifting.
xmr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Monero trades on {brand}: subaddresses and amount handling.

blurt.one_line: Coordination chain — transparent and account-based. Lowest privacy on {brand}.
blurt.intro: BLURT is Morphit's coordination chain — orders, chat ciphertexts, fees, and reputation all live here. The chain is fully public and account-based, meaning every BLURT transfer involving your account is permanently visible to anyone. There is no opt-in privacy technology for BLURT.
blurt.caveats: BLURT is structurally the least private asset on {brand}. Your account name is your address; you cannot rotate it. For trades where on-chain privacy matters more than speed and cost, prefer XMR, BTC (with PayJoin), BCH (with CashFusion), LTC (with MWEB), or DASH (with PrivateSend).
blurt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for BLURT trades on {brand}: account-based chain, transparent by design.

usdt.one_line: Centralized — Tether can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdt.intro: USDT's privacy issue is structurally different from the other transparent assets: it's centralized. Tether Inc. can freeze any USDT address on any host chain, and they have used this ability in the past. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Tether's freeze capability.
usdt.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDT remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDT host chains (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BSC) is the same as on any transparent EVM/UTXO/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem (Tornado Cash on ETH, etc.), which we do not endorse or describe further here.
usdt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDT trades on {brand}: centralization risk and host-chain transparency.

bch.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — CashFusion provides opt-in mixing.
bch.intro: Bitcoin Cash shares Bitcoin's transparency model: every transaction visible on chain, every address linkable. CashFusion (a BCH-community CoinJoin variant with amount-randomization) is the main opt-in privacy technology and is well-integrated into several BCH wallets.
bch.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin Cash trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, CashFusion, and what to avoid.

ltc.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — MWEB provides opt-in chain-level privacy.
ltc.intro: Litecoin shares Bitcoin's transparency at the base layer, but adds MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks) — a chain-level opt-in privacy feature that hides amounts and breaks address linkability for transfers that opt in. This is the closest a Bitcoin-family chain comes to native privacy.
ltc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Litecoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, MWEB, and what to avoid.

dash.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized — PrivateSend provides masternode-coordinated opt-in mixing.
dash.intro: Dash forked from Litecoin in 2014 and shares the same transparent base layer — every address balance and transaction is publicly visible. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer can freeze addresses. Dash adds PrivateSend, a CoinJoin variant coordinated by the masternode network, providing opt-in mixing at the wallet level. Pre-mixing several rounds before sharing your receiving address is the strongest privacy practice on Dash.
dash.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dash trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, PrivateSend pre-mixing, and what to avoid.
dash.caveats: PrivateSend's anonymity set depends on simultaneous mixing participants. Off-peak hours = smaller set = weaker unlinkability. Masternode coordination is a trust trade-off: the protocol is non-custodial (masternodes never hold your coins) but the coordinator sees the mixing pattern.

usdc.one_line: Centralized — Circle can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdc.intro: USDC's privacy posture mirrors USDT's: it's centralized. Circle (USDC's issuer) can freeze any USDC address on any host chain, and has done so on regulatory request. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Circle's freeze capability. The amount-correlation defense (jitter) IS active for USDC trades — see /{lang}/faq#monero_amount_jitter — but jitter addresses a different threat than centralization.
usdc.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDC remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDC host chains (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon) is the same as on any transparent EVM/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem, which we do not endorse or describe further here. BEP-20 USDC on BNB Chain is intentionally NOT supported: that variant is Binance-Peg (Binance-custodied wrapper of Circle-issued USDC), adding a second custodian to the existing one.
usdc.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDC trades on {brand}: centralization risk, host-chain transparency, and the amount-jitter defense.

dai.one_line: DAI — USD-pegged stablecoin governed by MakerDAO. No admin freeze on the token, but partly backed by USDC.
dai.meta_description: Honest privacy notes for trading DAI on {brand}: more decentralized than USDT/USDC at the contract level, partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module.
dai.intro: DAI is MakerDAO's USD-pegged stablecoin, deployed on Ethereum and several other EVM chains. It's the most-decentralized US-dollar-pegged asset {brand} supports — but "decentralized" doesn't mean "freeze-immune" or "fully crypto-backed" anymore. This page is the honest picture so you can choose with eyes open.

doge.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized via PoW, no native privacy upgrade.
doge.intro: Dogecoin launched in 2013 as a fair-launched fork of an earlier Litecoin variant. Like Bitcoin, every address balance and transaction is publicly visible on the chain. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer or foundation can freeze addresses. Since 2014 it has been merge-mined with Litecoin (auxiliary proof-of-work), inheriting Litecoin's hashrate security without competing for it.
doge.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dogecoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, avoiding chain heuristics, and what tradeoffs to expect.
doge.caveats: Dogecoin has no native privacy upgrade — no PrivateSend equivalent, no confidential transactions, no segwit-enabled mixing. Every receive address you publish on {brand} can be linked to its on-chain history forever. Use a fresh HD-derived address for every trade (your wallet usually does this automatically).

zec.one_line: Transparent and shielded address types coexist; recipients pick per address.
zec.intro: Zcash launched in 2016 as the first deployment of zk-SNARK-based shielded transactions in a cryptocurrency. The chain supports two address families: transparent (t1/t3) which behave like Bitcoin's legacy addresses with publicly visible amounts, and shielded (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address bundling Orchard receivers) which use zero-knowledge proofs to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Per-trade, the recipient picks the address type that matches their preferred posture. Both are first-class on the protocol.
zec.meta_description: Privacy practices for Zcash trades on {brand}: choosing between transparent and shielded addresses (t-addr, z-addr, u-addr), wallet recommendations, and what each privacy pool does.
zec.caveats: Shielded-to-shielded transactions hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Mixed transactions (shielded-to-transparent or transparent-to-shielded) reveal one side. Transparent-to-transparent reveals both. If your goal is to minimize linkability, use a shielded address (zs1 or u1) and ask the counterparty to send from a shielded address. Wallet support varies: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk (mobile, Sapling) — not every wallet supports every address type, so verify your counterparty's wallet handles the address type you publish before sharing it.

arrr.one_line: Chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool; every transfer hides sender, recipient, and amount by construction.
arrr.intro:
Pirate Chain (ARRR) launched in 2018 as a fork of the Zcash codebase, configured so that the Sapling shielded pool is the only available transaction type.  Every transfer goes through zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) that hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain.  Pirate Chain sunsetted the transparent pool early in the chain's life and forcibly migrated all transparent balances to shielded — there is no transparent address option.  Addresses use the `zs1` Sapling format (bech32, 78 chars total), visually identical to Zcash Sapling addresses.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene that survives even chain-level shielding — the on-chain payload is private, but what you share off-chain (which addresses you publish, which counterparties you transact with) is what links your {brand} trades together over time.
arrr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Pirate Chain trades on {brand}: chain-level shielded transactions, fresh-address hygiene, and wallet compatibility.
arrr.caveats:
Pirate Chain's chain-level shielding hides sender, recipient, and amount on chain — but it does not erase off-chain linkability.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `zs1` address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders even though the chain itself reveals nothing.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Pirate Chain wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Wallet compatibility.**  Not every wallet supports Pirate Chain (the major options are Treasure Chest, Pirate.Black, and Verus-integrated Pirate).  Confirm your counterparty has a compatible wallet before agreeing to a price.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Visual collision with Zcash Sapling addresses.**  Pirate Chain `zs1` addresses look exactly like Zcash `zs1` addresses.  {brand}'s per-asset tab and placeholder disambiguate, but if you copy an address from a different context, confirm it belongs to the chain you intend to send on.

dcr.one_line: Hybrid PoW/PoS cryptocurrency with on-chain governance (Politeia) and opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) wallet-side mixing.
dcr.intro:
Decred (DCR) launched in 2016 as a hybrid Proof-of-Work + Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with on-chain governance.  Every block is mined by PoW miners AND voted on by 5 PoS ticket-holders chosen pseudo-randomly from the staking pool — neither group can change the protocol rules unilaterally.  On-chain governance via Politeia lets stakeholders propose, debate, and ratify protocol changes; treasury funds (10% of block reward) flow through community vote.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Decred ships an opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing protocol integrated into dcrwallet: users can enable mixing in their wallet to break the on-chain transaction graph between deposit and withdrawal, similar in posture to Bitcoin coinjoin or Dash PrivateSend.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene to make the most of Decred's privacy features.
dcr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Decred trades on {brand}: hybrid PoW/PoS chain, on-chain governance, opt-in CoinShuffle++ wallet mixing, and fresh-address hygiene.
dcr.caveats:
Decred is transparent at the base layer; mixing is opt-in and wallet-side.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `Ds` or `Dc` address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Decred wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Use CSPP mixing if you want transaction-level privacy.**  In dcrwallet enable the "Mix Account" option; deposits flow through CoinShuffle++ rounds with other participants before becoming spendable from your mixed account.  Mixing rounds happen approximately every 20 minutes on mainnet.
- **Wallet compatibility.**  The official wallets are dcrwallet (CLI/headless), Decrediton (GUI), and Cake Wallet (mobile, DCR mode).  Some other wallets support DCR send/receive but not CSPP mixing.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Politeia treasury proposals are public.**  Decred's on-chain governance system shows every proposal, vote, and discussion publicly.  This isn't a Morphit-trading concern, but worth knowing if you participate in DCR governance.

sol.one_line: High-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with Proof-of-History sequencing.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
sol.intro:
Solana (SOL) launched in 2020 as a high-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Validators stake SOL and process blocks in rotation under delegated PoS consensus, with Proof-of-History providing a verifiable sequencing oracle that lets validators reach consensus on transaction ordering without coordination overhead.  The combination achieves transaction throughput several orders of magnitude higher than traditional UTXO chains while remaining decentralized — no central freeze authority controls the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Solana has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
sol.meta_description: Privacy practices for Solana trades on {brand}: high-throughput PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped SOL, and RPC provider considerations.
sol.caveats:
Solana is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Solana address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Solana wallets (Phantom, Solflare) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native SOL, not wrapped SOL.**  Wrapped SOL (wSOL) uses the SPL-token form for DEX interoperability; the mint address `So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112` is the famous wSOL identifier.  {brand} trades use NATIVE SOL transfers — sending wSOL to a SOL receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for Program-Derived Addresses (PDAs).**  PDAs are off-curve addresses controlled by on-chain programs, not by private keys.  If you send SOL to a PDA, the recipient can't move funds out unless the owning program has a withdraw instruction.  Most wallets show a warning before sending to a PDA; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as USDT-Solana and USDC-Solana.**  A Solana base58 address could be a native SOL account, a USDT-Solana token account, or a USDC-Solana token account — the format is identical.  {brand}'s order asset field tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Solana RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Helius, QuickNode, Triton, public mainnet-beta) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a Solana RPC node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.

eth.one_line: Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency on the Ethereum mainnet.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
eth.intro:
Ethereum (ETH) launched in 2015 as a smart-contract platform.  In September 2022 the chain transitioned from Proof-of-Work to Proof-of-Stake consensus ("The Merge") — validators stake ETH and process blocks in rotation, with no central freeze authority controlling the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Ethereum has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Tornado Cash was a notable smart-contract mixer but has been sanctioned in many jurisdictions; {brand} does not recommend or rely on it.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
eth.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ethereum trades on {brand}: PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped ETH, contract-destination warnings, ENS limitations, and RPC provider considerations.
eth.caveats:
Ethereum is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Ethereum address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Ethereum wallets (MetaMask, Rabby, Rainbow) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native ETH, not wrapped ETH.**  Wrapped ETH (WETH) is an ERC-20 token used for DEX interoperability.  {brand} trades use NATIVE ETH transfers — sending WETH to an ETH receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for contract destinations.**  Ethereum addresses can be externally-owned accounts (EOAs, controlled by a private key) OR smart contracts.  Sending ETH to a contract without a `payable receive()` or `fallback()` function reverts; the funds aren't lost but the transaction fails and you pay gas.  Most wallets warn before sending to contracts; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as every EVM token-account.**  An Ethereum 0x-address could be a native ETH EOA, a USDT-ERC20 token-account, a USDC-Base token-account, a DAI-Polygon token-account, or any EVM contract.  The format is identical.  {brand}'s order asset field (plus the network field for multi-network assets) tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **ENS names are not resolved.**  Pasting `alice.eth` will fail {brand}'s address validator — paste the raw 0x address.  Resolving ENS would require a centralized RPC dependency that violates Morphit's distributed-no-SPOF design.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Ethereum RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Infura, Alchemy, QuickNode, public mainnet) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting an Ethereum node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Gas fees can leak timing.**  Ethereum gas prices vary by congestion.  Submitting a transaction during a high-gas window with a higher tip can correlate the tx to a specific time window.  Standard wallet defaults (medium priority) blend with the broader mempool.

xrp.one_line: Federated Byzantine Agreement cryptocurrency on the XRP Ledger.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
xrp.intro:
Ripple (XRP) launched in 2012 as a payment-focused cryptocurrency.  XRPL uses Federated Byzantine Agreement (FBA) consensus — validators on a Unique Node List (UNL) reach agreement on transaction ordering.  The default UNL is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation (non-profit) with the for-profit Ripple Labs Inc. historically influencing validator selection.  Native XRP cannot be frozen by any central authority — the freeze flag on XRPL applies only to issued tokens (IOUs), not to native XRP.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, amount, and destination tag (if present) are all visible on chain like Bitcoin.  XRPL has no native protocol-level mixing.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
xrp.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ripple (XRP) trades on {brand}: XRPL FBA consensus, transparent base layer, destination tag UX, reserve requirement, and RPC provider considerations.
xrp.caveats:
XRPL is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same XRPL address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern XRPL wallets (Xaman, Crossmark, Bifrost) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Destination tags are not a privacy feature — they're an identifier, and {brand} cannot carry one.** A tag is visible on chain and correlates transactions. {brand}'s address share has no tag field and its payment link sets none, so never share an exchange-hosted deposit address that needs a tag (the funds would be lost in the exchange's pool); share a self-custody address that needs no tag.
- **Reserve requirement creates account-creation visibility.**  Your first incoming XRP must be ≥1 XRP (the base reserve).  The on-chain `Payment` transaction that funds a new account is publicly visible as account activation, which is a stronger correlation signal than a regular payment to an already-existing account.  If reducing this signal matters, fund the receive address yourself first (from an account that's already mixed/separated) and only then share it.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **XRPL RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an XRPL RPC endpoint (xrplcluster.com, Ripple's, or a self-hosted rippled node) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a rippled node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Consensus-set concentration is a known property.**  The default UNL (Unique Node List) is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation; running your own validator with a custom UNL is supported but uncommon.  For Morphit's purposes this affects censorship-resistance considerations (a coordinated UNL could refuse to include transactions) more than transaction privacy.  Document and decide based on your threat model.
- **Only classic addresses are accepted.** XRPL has a newer "X-address" format (XLS-5d) that bundles a destination tag into the address. {brand} accepts only classic `r`-prefixed addresses and carries no tag, so share a self-custody classic address that needs no tag.

privacy_terms.heading: Privacy & Terms
privacy_terms.privacy_body_1: {brand} runs in your browser. Your keys are generated on your device and never leave it. {brand} does not collect anything about you. Pick a memorable username, that's it.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_2: Every offer you post — along with the feedback and reviews you leave and receive — is public on the blockchain, for reputation-building, posterity, and your own research on other traders.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_protected: By contrast, your private conversations stay private. Direct messages between traders are end-to-end encrypted — they live on the blockchain only as ciphertext that you and your trade partner can read, never the operator, the indexers, or anyone else watching the chain. {brand} also collects no name, email, phone, or ID, and the payment details you exchange (such as a receiving address) move through that encrypted channel instead of the public orderbook.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_3: We encourage you to use a VPN, Tor, Lokinet, or I2P when accessing {brand} — anything that hides your IP from the server you're talking to is a good idea. We don't fingerprint your browser, we don't profile you, and we explicitly design our defenses against abuse so they don't punish privacy-conscious users. Our rate limits are crude (a handful of signups per user per day) and easily defeated by VPN rotation — that's a conscious tradeoff. We'd rather accept more abuse than make privacy-respecting users feel unwelcome. If a defense would require tracking you to work, we don't ship it.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_zero_clearnet: We go further than encouraging privacy. A Morphit node can run with zero use of the clearnet internet: chain reads, BTC/XMR fee checks, prices, and software updates all travel over Tor and I2P, and on such a node a firewall rule lets only Tor and I2P reach the internet. The node claims this only when its own checks of every outbound path pass, and other nodes show it as that instance's own statement. It is per-node — a clearnet instance still uses clearnet by design. For someone in a censored region, that is a marketplace node that visitors reach only over Tor or I2P, and that does not go dark when a clearnet address is blocked.
privacy_terms.terms_body: Please abide by the Non-Aggression Principle (NAP). Cursing is acceptable, but just keep in mind that there are all ages that use {brand}. Elderly, teens and everyone in between. All OPINIONS are welcome here, but directed insults are not. Your buy/sell orders, your private chats and the feedback section are immutable, so wording is everything. State your opinion, then stop. Don't start fights. Do not post illegal or obviously objectionable stuff. Remember your manners, be nice. 💚💙

run_a_node.title: Run a Morphit node
run_a_node.subtitle_post: . Earn 90% of the BLURT paid listing fees!
run_a_node.why_uncensor_body: Every additional instance makes the network harder to censor. If your country blocks morphit.io, your instance stays reachable. You serve users who'd otherwise have no way to trade.
run_a_node.why_community_body: Brand the interface for your region, your language, your local payment methods. Users trust frontends that speak their language and feel familiar — yours will.
run_a_node.why_privacy_body: Users trading on your instance might share their request-level metadata with your server and not with anyone else. Their public trading activity (orders, encrypted chats, reviews) is on chain so everyone can verify it.
run_a_node.why_privacy_body_2: Encourage users to use a VPN and your (included) Tor and/or I2P addresses. Your alternate, hidden addresses let users reach your instance from jurisdictions where clearnet access is blocked. No SSL/https certificates are needed either and the impact is enormous for users in censored networks and countries.
run_a_node.why_earn_body:
Every BLURT-paid listing fee your instance attracts pays you 90% — only 10% goes to the Morphit treasury to fund development and maintenance of the Morphit software.

No middleman can access your money: each fee is paid as two automated blockchain transfers — 90% straight to your fees account, 10% to the treasury.

Payouts are in BLURT, so if BLURT appreciates, so do your earnings — without any additional work on your part.
run_a_node.step1_title: Get a machine and a web address
run_a_node.step1_body: A cheap VPS or an old PC/laptop running Ubuntu — aim for 4 GB of RAM or more (8 GB is comfy) and 80 GB of disk. A Raspberry Pi 4 works too. Add a domain name (about $10/year) from any registrar and point it at the machine. Hosting from home? No static IP needed — the setup wizard turns on dynamic-DNS for you.
run_a_node.step3_title: Tell the world about your site
run_a_node.step3_body: You instantly appear in the /operators and /instances directories and you start earning the 90% share of the Blurt-paid listing fees on your site automatically. See the operator-earnings FAQ for the economics.
run_a_node.asset_policy_heading: Your instance, your asset and payment-methods policies
run_a_node.asset_policy_body: The federation lets each Operator pick which tradable assets their site supports. You can opt out per-asset and even configure which payment methods your site should support such as Cash, Paypal, Klarna, etc.
run_a_node.asset_policy_federation_body: Disabling an asset on your instance doesn't hide peer instances' orders from your users — chain history is shared, so your orderbook can still show them.
run_a_node.req_hw_value: 2+ CPUs, 4+ GB RAM, 80+ GB drive space (SSD is best)
run_a_node.req_network_value: Home internet works fine — DDNS handles dynamic IPs, no static IP required

security.heading: Security posture
security.subtitle: What we promise, and what that means for you.
security.keys_title: Your keys never leave your device.
security.keys_body: Keys are generated in your browser using libsodium. They are encrypted with a password you choose (Argon2id + XSalsa20-Poly1305) before being stored. No Morphit server ever sees them.
security.tracking_body: No cookies. No analytics. No third-party scripts. No telemetry. Your IP address reaches the server you use, as with any website; Morphit's code keeps it only in memory for rate limiting and never writes it to disk or a log. Look at the Network tab in your browser: your orders, your chat, and your balances all go to {brand} and nowhere else.
security.zero_clearnet_title: A node can run with zero clearnet.
security.zero_clearnet_body: Morphit is built so an operator can run a node that does not use the clearnet internet. Its outbound paths ride Tor and I2P instead: chain reads over hidden-service RPC, BTC/XMR fee checks through block explorers that run as onion services, prices from Haveno and Bisq price servers on onion addresses and from the federation rather than a clearnet API, and upgrades from other operators' hidden IPFS gateways, checked against the signed on-chain hash. On such a node a firewall rule lets only the Tor and I2P programs reach the internet; anything else that tries is refused. (I2P works by talking to other I2P routers directly, so someone watching the server's line can see that it runs I2P.) The node claims zero clearnet only when its own checks of every outbound path pass, and other nodes show that claim as the instance's own statement: they cannot verify it. A server that once ran on clearnet stays linked to its old domain, so a node meant to stay hidden starts with fresh keys and a fresh operator account.
security.chat_body: Every message is locked with X25519 key agreement and ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption (libsodium primitives): a fresh one-time key per message combined with both parties' chat keys, so only you and your partner can open it, and your partner can tell it really came from you. Plaintext exists only in your browser and your partner's. Morphit's servers, the chain and anyone in between see only ciphertext — plus who talks to whom, when, and about which order. The full design, including what we deliberately do not provide (forward secrecy), is in {chat_crypto_doc}.
security.reproducible_body: Every release is built from a signed git tag, and @morphit anchors on the Blurt chain the SHA-256 of its source tarball together with the hashes of the files that start the website (page shell, service worker, entry code). Your browser compares the copies it loaded with that signed list. That catches a file changed by accident or by a partly compromised server; it cannot protect you from a hostile operator, who serves the checking code too. There is no Subresource Integrity on the scripts, and builds are not byte-for-byte reproducible yet, so you verify a download by its hash and signature (docs/VERIFY-YOUR-DOWNLOAD.md), not by rebuilding it.
security.open_source_body: The full threat model is in the repo's {security_doc}. We're explicit about what we protect against and what we don't — because pretending otherwise would be worse than honesty.
security.footer_body: Found a security issue? Send it only as a private Matrix message to @agorise:matrix.org. Never post the details in public: not in a Forgejo issue (issues there are public), not in a chat room, and not on the chain (a message to {morphit_account} there stays public forever).
security.bounty_body: We run a discretionary security recognition program. Every actionable finding gets reviewed by a real engineer, gets an answer, and — if it materially improves Morphit's security posture — gets rewarded in BLURT (paid from @morphit-fees) or BTC, scaled to severity and the report's quality. No fixed tier table; case-by-case adjudication. Hall of fame credit available even when payment isn't. The full scope, severity guidance, payment workflow, and what we won't do (no NDA, no exclusive disclosure) is documented in docs/SECURITY.md.
security.bounty_link: Read the full bounty program scope and rules
security.canary_body: We publish a weekly warrant canary signed with the operator's PGP key. The canary explicitly declares no NSL / FISA / gag-order / backdoor demand has been served. Freshness proofs include a current blockchain head, a current Bitcoin chain head, and a current news headline (proves the canary cannot be pre-generated). If the canary stops updating for more than 14 days, treat it as silent: the operator may be under coercive pressure, and you should switch to a different federated operator.

display_name.reminder_body: Anyone can use any name. The short key in parentheses is what really identifies you, and it cannot be copied by anyone else. Always check the key when you're trading.
display_name.broadcast_ok_detail: Your display name is now published for everyone to see.
display_name.clear_local_only: A published display name can't be removed yet; you can replace it with another name. Clearing it here changes this device only.

endpoints.heading: RPC endpoints
endpoints.explain: The nodes that this {brand} site talks to for syncing blockchain data, trying them in order of privacy and fastest response.
endpoints.err_rpc: Answered, but the RPC call failed
endpoints.err_transport_off: Requires Tor/I2P (not enabled on this instance)

session.heading: Utility
session.explain: Sign out when you're done. Your keys will be wiped from memory; the encrypted keystore on your device is untouched.
session.autolock_help: Automatically lock your session after this long with no activity. Locking clears your keys from memory; your encrypted keystore stays on this device so you can unlock with your password when you return.

change_password.heading: Change password
change_password.help: Replace your keystore password without signing out. Your keys stay the same; only the password that decrypts them changes.
change_password.strength_common: This password is too common. Pick something less guessable.
change_password.strength_trivial: This password is too simple. Try a longer mix of words.
change_password.strength_short: Consider a longer password — 12+ characters is much harder to guess.

err.new_password_too_short: New password must be at least 8 characters.
err.same_password: New password must be different from your current password.
err.locked: Your session is locked. Unlock first, then try again.
err.bad_old_password: That doesn't match your current password. Try again.
err.mismatch: The two new passwords don't match.
err.internal: Something went wrong. Your old password still works; please try again.

nostr_url.heading: Nostr link
nostr_url.explain: Add your Nostr profile URL here to help people reach you outside of {brand}. On your profile page, its linked icon is displayed next to your avatar.
nostr_url.label: Your Nostr URL
nostr_url.hint_empty: Paste your Nostr profile URL here, or leave blank.

error.too_long: Too long. Keep it under 512 characters.
error.invalid_scheme: Only nostr:, https://, and http:// URLs are allowed.
error.malformed: That does not look like a valid URL.

nostr_url.reminder_body: Your Morphit identity works fine without this URL. It's a courtesy link for people who might want to also see your Nostr profile.

website_url.heading: Website or Blog URL
website_url.explain: If you have a website or blog, paste the address to it here. On your profile page, its linked icon is displayed next to your avatar.
website_url.label: Website or blog URL
website_url.hint_empty: Paste your website or blog URL here, or leave blank.

error.invalid_scheme: URL must start with http:// or https://.

website_url.reminder_body: Your Morphit identity works fine without this URL. It's a courtesy link for people who might want to also see your profile content and images, etc.

streaming_url.heading: Streaming URL
streaming_url.explain: A link to your streaming profile (YouTube, Rumble, Blurt.media, Twitch, etc). On your profile page, its linked icon is displayed next to your avatar.
streaming_url.label: Streaming profile URL
streaming_url.hint_empty: Paste your videos/podcasts URL here, or leave blank.

error.invalid_scheme: URL must start with http:// or https://.

streaming_url.reminder_body: Your Morphit identity works fine without this URL. It's a courtesy link for people who might want to also see your videos or podcasts.

notifications.heading: Notifications
notifications.explain: {brand} pings you when something happens — an order fills, a chat message arrives, feedback lands. All of these are off-by-default where annoying-by-default, and opt-in where high-signal. Never when you're already looking at the page.
notifications.category_heading: What do you want to be told about?
notifications.category_order_help: Your order filled, expired, or was replaced by a counter-offer. Recommended on — highest signal-to-noise.
notifications.category_chat_help: New message in an active trade chat. Coalesced: 3 messages in 30 seconds is one notification.
notifications.category_feedback_help: Someone left you feedback, or responded to feedback you left them.
notifications.channel_ambient_help: Always on. Zero permissions, never audible. Works on the tab you're looking at.
notifications.channel_native_help: OS-native notification when a new event arrives and this tab isn't focused. Asks permission the first time we need it.
notifications.channel_push_help: Also notify when {brand} is not open at all. Requires a Web Push service.
notifications.channel_audio_help: Short sound when a notification fires. Only plays when this tab isn't focused.
notifications.channel_vibrate_help: Short vibration pattern when a notification fires. Ignored on devices that don't support it.
notifications.quiet_explain: No sound during these hours, and push notifications arrive silently (the browser still shows them). Visual channels (title bar, favicon, badge) still update — they're ambient, not alerts.
notifications.mute_until_unmute: Mute until I turn it back on
notifications.permission_banner_body: You just got a new {category} event. Want to know about future ones even when you're not looking at {brand}?
notifications.permission_denied_explain: You previously declined notifications. If you'd like to enable them, you'll need to change your browser's site permission for this page, then toggle the setting above.
notifications.hint_badging_unsupported: Your browser doesn't support OS-level app badges. Install {brand} as an app to enable this.
notifications.hint_notifications_unsupported: Your browser doesn't support desktop notifications.
notifications.push_error_push_disabled: This instance's operator has not enabled push delivery yet. Falling back to in-tab notifications.
notifications.push_error_push_disabled_hidden_only: This instance uses no clearnet at all, and phone and closed-browser notifications can only be delivered through a clearnet push service, so they are off here. Notifications still appear while {brand} is open.
notifications.push_error_permission_denied: You declined the browser's notification permission. To enable push later, allow notifications for this site in your browser settings.
notifications.push_error_not_supported: Your browser does not support Web Push. Try a recent Firefox, Chrome, or Edge.
notifications.push_error_unreachable: Could not reach the operator's relay. Check your connection and try again.
notifications.push_error_no_vapid_key: The operator's relay did not return a push key. Push may be temporarily disabled.
notifications.push_error_subscribe_failed: Subscription failed. Try again, or check your browser's site permissions.
notifications.push_error_internal: Something went wrong on the operator's relay. Try again in a moment.
notifications.push_error_signature_required: This instance requires a signed subscribe request. Make sure your account is unlocked and try again.
notifications.push_error_signature_invalid: Your signature was rejected by the relay. Try unlocking your account again, then retry.
notifications.push_error_locked_session: Your session is locked. Unlock your account first to enable push notifications.
notifications.push_error_push_service_unavailable: Your browser blocked web push — usually because the browser's push service is off or an ad/tracker blocker (like uBlock Origin) is blocking it. Check your browser's notification/privacy settings for this site and allow it, then try again. Or leave push off — the in-app badges still work when {brand} is open.
notifications.push_error_push_service_unavailable_brav: Brave blocks web push by default — it's a browser setting, not Shields. Fix it: open brave://settings/privacy, turn on "Use Google services for push messaging", relaunch Brave, then switch push on again here. (It routes through Google's servers — metadata only, never your message content.) Or leave push off; the in-app badges still work when {brand} is open.
notifications.push_error_push_service_unavailable_fire: Firefox blocked web push. Common causes: a Private window (push is off there — use a normal window), or Enhanced Tracking Protection (click the shield in the address bar and allow this site). Still stuck? Open about:config and set dom.push.enabled to true, then try again. Or leave push off; the in-app badges still work when {brand} is open.
notifications.push_error_push_service_unavailable_safa: Safari blocked web push. On Mac it needs macOS 13 (Ventura)+ and Safari 16+. Open Safari → Settings → Websites → Notifications, set morphit.io to Allow, then try again. On older macOS, use Chrome, Brave, or Firefox for push. Or leave push off; the in-app badges still work when {brand} is open.

hidden_accounts.heading: Hidden accounts
hidden_accounts.explain: Orders from these accounts don't appear on your orderbook view. You can unhide anyone at any time.
hidden_accounts.scope_note: Hiding is local to this browser. It doesn't ban anyone from the protocol, doesn't notify them, and doesn't affect what other Morphit instances see.
hidden_accounts.unhide_all_confirm: Unhide all {count} accounts? This will make their orders visible again on your orderbook view.

avatar.heading: Avatar
avatar.explain: Replace your default heart identicon with your own image.
avatar.guidance_filetypes: Accepts SVG, WebP, JPEG, PNG, or GIF.
avatar.guidance_dimensions: Ideal source: a square image at least 96×96 pixels. Anything larger will be resized down to 96×96 for you; anything smaller will look grainy.
avatar.guidance_filesize: Source file size: up to 5 MB. Larger images will be downsampled to 96×96 automatically, so even a phone photo straight from your camera works fine.
avatar.guidance_size: Raster images are automatically re-encoded to WebP at high quality. SVGs are minified losslessly. The final payload must fit under 6 KB.
avatar.guidance_svg_tips: SVG tip: a square viewBox (e.g. 0 0 100 100) renders best. Scripts, external references, and HTML-in-SVG are stripped automatically for security.
avatar.permanence_body: Once broadcast, your avatar is public on the blockchain forever. It cannot be deleted, only replaced. Never upload an image you wouldn't want publicly associated with your account for the rest of time — photos of faces, in particular, are a privacy consideration given modern face-recognition tools.

error.unsupported_type: That file type isn't supported. Use SVG, WebP, JPEG, PNG, or GIF.
error.input_too_large: That image is too large to upload. Please choose a file under 5 MB.
error.image_dimensions_too_large: That image's dimensions are too large to process (max 12000×12000, ~40 megapixels). Downscale it — most photos only need to be a few hundred pixels — and try again.
error.parse_failed: Couldn't parse this SVG. The file may be malformed.
error.svg_no_root: That doesn't look like a valid SVG file.
error.svg_too_large: This SVG is too complex to fit under the 6 KB on-chain limit. Try simplifying it — fewer paths, less detail, or a smaller viewBox.
error.raster_too_large: Even after resizing and re-encoding, this image is too large for on-chain storage. Try a simpler or less-detailed source image.
error.raster_decode_failed: Couldn't decode this image. The file may be corrupt or an unsupported format variant.
error.canvas_unavailable: Your browser doesn't support the image-processing features this needs. Try a different browser.
error.webp_unavailable: Your browser doesn't support WebP output. Try a different browser.
error.processing_failed: Couldn't process this image. Try a different file.

avatar.remove_confirm_body: This broadcasts a profile update that clears your avatar on-chain. You can upload a new one anytime.
avatar.preview_too_large: Too large to broadcast — the maximum is {cap}. Try a simpler image or a smaller source.

blocked_accounts.heading: Blocked accounts
blocked_accounts.explain: Accounts you have blocked cannot send you chat messages on Morphit. Blocking is on-chain and visible to anyone scraping Blurt, but {brand} does not tell the blocked person.
blocked_accounts.scope_note: This list is derived from on-chain blocks. Refresh to pull the latest from the indexer.
blocked_accounts.refresh_aria: Refresh the blocked accounts list from the indexer
blocked_accounts.unblock_failed: Could not unblock. Please check your connection and try again.
blocked_accounts.locked_hint: Unlock your session to unblock accounts.

syndication.heading: Syndication
syndication.explain: {brand} can publish announcement posts to your Blurt blog when you take certain actions. These are signed by your posting key.
syndication.first_trade_label: Announce my first trade to the @morphit community
syndication.first_trade_help: When you leave feedback for your first-ever Morphit trade, also publish a short "I joined Morphit" post to the @morphit community on Blurt. Posts only once per account, ever. Per-order syndication is a separate per-submission checkbox on the order form.
syndication.pitch_body: Syndication of your trades is everything. More eyes on your offers means more trading partners, plus upvote rewards going directly into your Blurt Wallet. Off = nothing public.
syndication.blog_default_explain: {brand} can now pre-tick the "post this order to my Blurt blog" box on every new order, so your offers get pushed out automatically. Each post is still signed by you, and you can untick it on any individual order.
syndication.blog_default_label: Post my orders to my Blurt blog by default

privacy.heading: Privacy
privacy.cross_page_trade_events_help: When on, {brand} watches your recent chats for trade events (address shared, funds sent) so badges update on /my/orders without you opening the chat. This briefly decrypts incoming messages in the background. Turn off if you prefer the chat page itself to be the only place trade events are processed.
privacy.address_history_help: Crypto addresses you share in chat are remembered on this device — as one-way fingerprints, not the addresses themselves, and without dates or orders — so {brand} can warn you if you reuse one. They stay in this browser only and are never sent to any server.
privacy.address_history_empty: No addresses remembered on this device yet.
privacy.address_history_forget_confirm: Forget all {count} remembered addresses? This clears them from this browser only and can't be undone.

hardware_key.heading: Hardware key
hardware_key.explain: Bind a YubiKey to your keystore as another way to unlock it, or as the only way. Only YubiKey-only mode stops someone who has your password.
hardware_key.unsupported_title: Your browser doesn't support hardware keys
hardware_key.unsupported_body: YubiKey unlock requires the WebHID API, which is not available for all web browsers. You can keep using your password as before.
hardware_key.seed_only_note: Hardware keys are only available when you have a persisted keystore. You're using seed-only mode — no envelope is stored on this device, so there's nothing to bind a key to.
hardware_key.soften_explain: After this, you'll be able to unlock with EITHER your YubiKey OR a password. Set a new password below; you'll need your YubiKey one more time to apply the change.
hardware_key.backup_warning_title: Have you backed up your seed phrase and your keys?
hardware_key.backup_warning_body: Adding a YubiKey re-encrypts your keystore. If you lose access to your YubiKey AND forget your password, only your 12-word seed phrase can recover this account. Please make sure it's written down somewhere safe before continuing.
hardware_key.backup_confirm_label: Yes, my seed phrase is backed up safely.
hardware_key.slot_hint: Most users program HMAC-SHA1 challenge-response into slot 2 — slot 1 usually holds Yubico OTP. Use YubiKey Manager to configure your key first if you haven't already.
hardware_key.harden_warning_title: This is a one-way switch — proceed with care.
hardware_key.harden_warning_body: After hardening, your password will no longer unlock this keystore. Only your YubiKey will. If you lose your YubiKey, only your 12-word seed phrase can recover this account. You can always soften back later, but it requires a YubiKey tap.
hardware_key.harden_confirm_label: I understand. Without my YubiKey or seed phrase, this account is permanently inaccessible.

phase.requesting: Choose your YubiKey from the browser prompt…

error.enroll_verify_failed: We couldn't verify your YubiKey. Make sure slot 2 is set up for HMAC-SHA1 challenge-response, try a different USB port, then enroll again.
error.confirm_backup: Please confirm your seed phrase is backed up before continuing.
error.webhid_unsupported: Your browser doesn't support WebHID. Try Chrome, Edge, or Brave.
error.open_failed: Couldn't open the YubiKey. Make sure it's plugged in and not in use by another app.
error.timeout: YubiKey timed out. Tap your key promptly when it lights up.
error.persist_failed: Couldn't save the change to this device. Storage may be unavailable (private mode, quota, or disabled). The change has not been applied.
error.unknown: Something went wrong. Try again, and if the problem persists, restart the page.
error.label_too_long: The label you entered is too long.
error.wrap_limit_reached: This keystore already has the maximum number of YubiKey wraps. Remove one before adding another.
error.duplicate_yubikey_label: This keystore already has a YubiKey enrolled. Remove the existing one first to add a different YubiKey.
error.not_layered: This keystore isn't ready for hardware-key operations. Enroll a YubiKey first.
error.no_yubikey_wrap: This keystore has no YubiKey enrolled.
error.wrap_index_out_of_range: That YubiKey wrap couldn't be found. Reload the page and try again.
error.cannot_unenroll_last_wrap: Removing this would leave your keystore unrecoverable. Add another unlock method first.
error.protocol_violation: YubiKey responded with a malformed packet. Try a different USB port or cable. If the problem persists, try a different YubiKey.
error.unsafe_kdf_params: This keystore was saved with weakened security parameters and may have been tampered with. Re-enroll your YubiKey to write a fresh, safe envelope.

error.unwrap_failed: Couldn't decrypt the keystore with this YubiKey. Make sure you tapped the correct key, or try a different one if you've enrolled multiple.

install.heading: Install {brand} as an app
install.explain: Add {brand} to your home screen for one-tap access. The app launches in fullscreen, works offline, and gets the same updates as the website. No data leaves your device that wouldn't already.
install.manual_intro: Your browser doesn't expose a one-click install. Use the manual path:
install.manual_chrome: Chrome / Edge: tap the address bar's install icon, or use the browser menu → Install {brand}.
install.manual_safari: Safari (macOS / iOS): tap the Share button, then "Add to Home Screen".
install.manual_firefox: Firefox Android: tap the menu (︙), then "Install". Firefox desktop doesn't support PWA install — use Chromium-based browsers.

account_name.heading: Account name
account_name.explain: {brand} needs to know your account name so it can recognize your trades, messages, and on-chain activity. If you imported a posting key with the account name, this is already set. If you imported a seed phrase or keyfile, set it here.
account_name.locked_explain: To change this, sign out, then re-import with a different account.
account_name.input_hint: Without the @. We'll verify your posting key matches this account on the blockchain before saving.
account_name.error_locked: Unlock your keystore first to set your account name.
account_name.error_bad_format: Account names use lowercase letters, digits, dashes, and dots — 3 to 16 characters, starting with a letter.
account_name.error_not_found: We couldn't find @{account} on the blockchain. Check the spelling.
account_name.error_key_mismatch: Your posting key doesn't match @{account}'s posting authority. Check that you imported the right keys.
account_name.error_chain_unreachable: We couldn't reach the blockchain. Check your connection and try again.
account_name.no_account_link: Don't have an account yet? Claim a name

import_landing_banner.title: Almost done — pick your @account so the orderbook recognizes you
import_landing_banner.body: We brought you here because seed/keyfile imports don't carry your account name. Set it once below and we'll verify it on-chain.

preferences.heading: Preferences
preferences.explain: {brand} remembers a few of your form values so you don't have to refill them every time you post. Stored only on this device — never sent to any server, never put on chain.
preferences.empty: No preferences saved yet. Post an order and your fiat currency and region will be remembered for next time.
preferences.clear_confirm_body: Clear your saved fiat currency and region? You'll just need to pick them again next time you post.

totp.heading: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
totp.subtitle: Add an authenticator app as a second factor after your password. Protects against shoulder-surfing, borrowed devices, and casual local malware.

honest_framing.title: What this protects against — honestly
honest_framing.protects_intro: TOTP-based 2FA is a meaningful second gate after your password. It stops:
honest_framing.protects_shoulder_surf: Someone watching you type your password
honest_framing.protects_borrowed: A friend who watched you log in once trying again on your laptop
honest_framing.protects_malware: Casual local malware that grabs your keystore but doesn’t know to extract the TOTP secret
honest_framing.limits_intro: It does NOT add cryptographic strength against:
honest_framing.limits_offline: A determined attacker who has stolen your encrypted keystore AND cracked your password — the TOTP secret lives in the same encrypted blob as the keys.
honest_framing.limits_path_forward: For a factor whose secret never lives in the keystore, use a YubiKey in YubiKey-only mode (Settings → Hardware key): then neither your password nor a copy of the keystore file unlocks your keys without the key in your hand.

status.backup_codes_remaining: {count, plural, one {# backup code remaining} other {# backup codes remaining}}
status.backup_codes_low: You’re running low on backup codes. Regenerate a new set and put them somewhere safe.
status.backup_codes_exhausted: You have no backup codes left. If you lose your authenticator, you’ll need your seed phrase to recover.

enroll.step1_body: We strongly recommend the open-source options below. {brand} does NOT recommend Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, or Authy — closed source, with backup/sync paths that can leak your secrets.
enroll.step2_body: Open your authenticator and scan this code. If you can’t scan (no camera, accessibility), enter the secret manually below.
enroll.step3_title: 3. Confirm the code from your app
enroll.step3_body: Type the 6-digit code your authenticator currently shows. The code rotates every 30 seconds; if yours just changed, wait for the next one.
enroll.step4_body: These ten codes will let you log in if you lose your authenticator. Each code works exactly ONCE. Save them somewhere safe — a password manager, printed and locked away, or written on paper. We will not show them again.
enroll.backup_acknowledge: I have saved these backup codes somewhere safe.
enroll.err_invalid_code: That code didn’t verify. Check your device time is in sync and try again.
enroll.err_internal: Something went wrong. Your keystore is unchanged; please try again.
enroll.err_locked: Your session is locked. Unlock first, then try again.

unenroll.confirm_body: You’ll be able to unlock with just your password. Are you sure?
unenroll.err_invalid_code: That code didn’t verify. Try again.

regenerate.confirm_body: Your previous backup codes will stop working immediately. Make sure you can complete the new-codes save step before continuing.
regenerate.err_invalid_code: That code didn’t verify. Try again.

unlock_prompt.body: Your keystore opened. Now enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app, or a backup code.
unlock_prompt.err_invalid_code: That code didn’t verify, or was already used. Wait for the next code, check your device time is in sync, or try a backup code.
unlock_prompt.err_locked_out: Too many invalid attempts. Try again in {seconds} seconds.
unlock_prompt.err_unavailable_insecure: Authenticator codes can’t be checked over this connection — your browser switches that feature off on plain-HTTP addresses such as I2P. Enter one of your backup codes instead, or unlock at the https:// or .onion address of {brand}.

aegis.tagline: Encrypted local backups, biometric lock, no cloud sync. Android only.

2fas.tagline: iOS + Android. Optional encrypted cloud backup is OPT-IN, not the default.

ente.tagline: End-to-end-encrypted cross-device sync (iOS + Android + Linux + Mac + Windows + Web).

not_recommended_apps.heading: Apps we don’t recommend (and why)
not_recommended_apps.expand: See which apps we suggest avoiding

google_authenticator.name: Google Authenticator
google_authenticator.reason: Closed source. Cloud backup syncs secrets to Google by default (opt-OUT, not opt-IN) and these secrets are not end-to-end encrypted to your account password.

authy.name: Authy
authy.reason: Closed source. Cloud-only backups with a history of account-recovery exploits (SIM-swap vectors). Desktop app deprecated 2024.

lost_device.heading: What if I lose my authenticator?
lost_device.body: Use one of your 10 backup codes at unlock. Each works once. If you lose your authenticator AND all backup codes, you’ll need your 12-word seed phrase to recover — there’s no admin who can help, because {brand} doesn’t hold your keys.

totp.yubikey_protected: This keystore is protected with a YubiKey. Adding TOTP-based 2FA to a YubiKey-protected keystore isn’t supported in this version. Your YubiKey already provides cryptographically stronger authentication than TOTP would.
totp.unavailable_insecure: Setting up two-factor authentication needs a browser feature that is switched off on this connection (a plain-HTTP address such as I2P). To turn 2FA on or off, or to get new backup codes, open {brand} at its https:// address, or at its .onion address in Tor Browser.

visibility.public_detail: Saved openly on the blockchain — anyone can read it, permanently.
visibility.private_detail: Encrypted before it leaves your device. Not even the operator can read it.
visibility.device_detail: Stays in this browser. Never sent anywhere.

preferred_language.title: Preferred languages
preferred_language.help: Choose the languages you want to see orders in. Your primary language is also the default for new orders you post.

settings.profile_load_failed: Your published profile couldn't be loaded, so publishing changes is paused: a field this page didn't load would be sent empty and erase it. You can still save on this device.

shipment_modal.heading: Record a shipment
shipment_modal.intro: Share your carrier + tracking number so your trade partner can verify the shipment.
shipment_modal.safety_heading: Safety tips for any physical shipment
shipment_modal.safety_insurance: Use a tracked, INSURED service. If the package is lost or stolen, insurance is your only recourse.
shipment_modal.safety_plain_envelope: Use a plain envelope or box with no markings suggesting valuables inside.
shipment_modal.safety_return_address: Return address tradeoff: omitting it preserves anonymity but means undeliverable mail gets destroyed.
shipment_modal.safety_tracking_optional: Add the carrier's tracking number — it is required, and it is your proof of shipment.
shipment_modal.cash_tips_toggle: If you're mailing CASH, read this first
shipment_modal.cash_tinfoil: Wrap the cash in aluminum foil inside the envelope — defeats people holding envelopes to bright light to see contents.
shipment_modal.cash_ups_fedex_prohibit: UPS and FedEx PROHIBIT cash shipments in their terms of service. If opened, they can confiscate with no recourse. Use a postal service instead.
shipment_modal.cash_customs: International: do not lie on customs declarations. High-value cash will be seized regardless.
shipment_modal.custom_tracking_url_help: Full https:// URL where the recipient can look up the tracking number.
shipment_modal.tracking_help: As provided by the carrier. Letters, numbers, spaces, dashes are accepted.

problem.carrier_invalid: Pick the carrier you shipped with.
problem.tracking_invalid: Enter the tracking number: 5 to 50 letters, digits, spaces, dashes or slashes.
problem.custom_carrier_name_too_long: The carrier name is too long (at most 100 characters).
problem.custom_tracking_url_invalid: The tracking link must be a full https:// address (at most 500 characters).
problem.note_too_long: The note is too long (at most 500 characters).
problem.note_forbidden_chars: The note contains a tab, line break or another invisible control character. Remove it and try again.
problem.order_permlink_invalid: This shipment can't be linked to the order. Close this window and open it again from the order.

shipment_modal.send_failed: The shipment could not be sent. Check your connection and try again.

support.heading: Help & support
support.subtitle: Most questions are answered in the FAQ. For anything else, here's how to reach the right place.

faq.heading: Search the FAQ
faq.body: How to trade, fees, lost keys, privacy, taxes — most everyday questions are already answered.

operator.heading: Contact this instance's operator
operator.body_with_name: {name} runs this instance. For trouble using the site, account-creation issues, or operator-specific questions, reach out to them directly.
operator.body_generic: An operator runs this instance. For trouble using the site, account-creation issues, or operator-specific questions, reach out via the contact link below.
operator.no_contact_hint: This operator hasn't published a contact link. Try the security disclosure or self-host options below.

security.heading: Found a security issue?
security.body: Bugs that put users at risk go to the project, not just this operator. We have a bug bounty program with a private disclosure channel.

self_host.heading: Run your own instance

welcome_first_buy.heading: Your first trade is on us. 🌱
welcome_first_buy.lead: Welcome to {brand}! Your first order is a free buy of BLURT — we cover the listing fee, and you walk away with a real starter balance in your wallet. Here's why this is one of the best onboarding deals in P2P crypto:
welcome_first_buy.bullet_free: The listing fee is free. Morphit pays the network fee for your first trade — your only cost is whatever you agree to pay your counterparty.
welcome_first_buy.bullet_starter: You walk away with actual funds in your on-chain wallet for the trading fees (at the discounted rate too (~12.5¢ each)) from day one.
welcome_first_buy.bullet_runway: BLURT works across the entire Blurt social network. Use it to vote on posts at blurt.blog, blurt.media, etc and earn rewards just by clicking "Like" on good content.
welcome_first_buy.bullet_bp_stake: Your 1 BP welcome stake is set aside when you pay your first listing fee in BLURT, and lent with your loyalty rewards once they reach the chain's minimum (about 34 BP). Your first completed trade on a listing you paid for brings 10 BLURT + 10 BLURT Power — a passive-income producing stake on the network.
welcome_first_buy.why_blurt_minimum: Why BLURT and not BTC or XMR for the free trade? Because the BLURT in your wallet is what lets you do everything else on {brand} afterward — pay listing fees on future trades (at half price!), participate in the Blurt social layer, and earn loyalty rewards. We want you set up to be active, not stranded with an empty balance.

unlock_active.title: This payment needs your Active key
unlock_active.body: You're signed in to @{account} with your Posting key only, which can't move money. Paste your Active key into the field to continue.
unlock_active.field_help: {brand} checks it against your account on the blockchain before signing anything. It never leaves this device.

error.invalid_wif: That doesn't look like a valid key. Check for a missing or extra character.
error.is_posting_key: That's your Posting key — the one you're already signed in with. It can't move money. Paste your Active key instead.
error.is_owner_key: That's your Owner key. It can take over your whole account, so {brand} will never use it. Please use your Active key.
error.not_this_account: That isn't this account's Active key. Check you're using the key for @{account}.
error.lookup_failed: Couldn't reach the blockchain to check your key. Try again in a moment.
error.bad_device_password: That {brand} password is wrong. Your Active key was not saved.
error.keep_failed: Couldn't save your Active key on this device. Nothing was changed — try again, or choose “Forget it”.

unlock_active.retention_once_help: Used once to sign, then erased from memory. You'll enter it again next time.
unlock_active.retention_keep: Keep it on this device, encrypted
unlock_active.retention_keep_help: Unlocked with your {brand} password from now on. Anyone who learns that password could then spend your BLURT, so only do this on a device you control.
unlock_active.device_password_help: The password you already unlock {brand} with. It encrypts your Active key on this device.

trust_score.heading: Why {score} and not the average?
trust_score.what_it_is: The {score} is a trust score. It doesn't take an average at face value — it starts everyone near 3.00 and only lets you climb toward your true average as you rack up more trades. Five perfect ratings gets you most of the way there, not all the way.
trust_score.why: Why bother? Otherwise I do three fake trades with my friend, we give each other 5 stars, and I instantly look as trustworthy as someone with 200 real trades at 4.9. The trust score makes a spotless record earned rather than claimed.
trust_score.drift: As real trades pile up, {score} can drift up toward the plain average on its own.

insecure_context.notice: Your browser doesn’t treat this address as a secure connection (a plain-HTTP I2P address, for example), so it switches off a few features here: authenticator (2FA) codes, copy buttons, the fingerprint check in chat, offline mode and notifications. Your keys, trading and chat still work. For those features, open {brand} at its https:// address, or at its .onion address in Tor Browser.

btc_fee_pay.heading: Pay the listing fee
btc_fee_pay.intro: Send the amount below to this Bitcoin address. The address belongs to this listing only, so nobody else can use your payment.
btc_fee_pay.waiting_address: Getting your payment address… This takes about a minute while the Blurt network confirms your order.
btc_fee_pay.mismatch: We couldn't double-check this payment address, so we're not showing it. Please don't pay yet: try again in a few minutes, or use another instance.
btc_fee_pay.on_its_way: We can see {amount} BTC on its way. The Bitcoin network usually confirms it within 10 to 60 minutes.
btc_fee_pay.all_sent: Payment received. As soon as the Bitcoin network confirms it, your order goes live by itself.
btc_fee_pay.paid: Fee paid. Your order is on the orderbook.
btc_fee_pay.when_live: You can close this page: your order goes live by itself once the payment is confirmed. Please pay within 7 days. You'll also find this address under My orders.
btc_fee_pay.slow: Still no address? Then your order was not accepted — and you have not paid anything. A reason can be the limit of 3 listings with a Bitcoin fee per day. Try again later, or pay the fee in BLURT.
btc_fee_pay.peer_disagrees: Another Morphit server gave this listing a different Bitcoin address, so this server's copy of the blockchain may be out of step. To keep your money safe we are not showing an address. Please try again later or open this listing on another Morphit server.

rewards.heading: What you get on {brand}
rewards.intro: Each reward is paid on the Blurt chain by this site's relay, usually a minute or so after the chain records what earned it (top-ups are checked every few hours).
rewards.free_account_body: We pay the chain's account fee (about 100 BLURT) and put 2 BLURT in your wallet to start.
rewards.free_buy_body: Your very first order can be a buy of at least $1 of BLURT with no listing fee. Post any other order first and this offer is gone.
rewards.welcome_stake_body: When you pay your first listing fee in BLURT, 1 BLURT Power is set aside for you. Blurt lends at least about 34 BP at a time, so it is lent together with your loyalty rewards once they add up to that.
rewards.first_trade_body: When your first trade on a listing you paid for is completed and your trade partner leaves you feedback (any rating), you receive 10 BLURT plus 10 BLURT powered up. Both are yours.
rewards.loyalty_body: As your BLURT listing fees add up to 100, 500, 2,000 and 10,000 BLURT, you are lent 10, 50, 200 and 1,000 BLURT Power more. Rewards below the chain's minimum (about 34 BP) are lent once your total reaches it, usually at the 500 BLURT milestone (61 BP).
rewards.top_up_body: If you posted an order here in the last week and your balance drops below 0.5 BLURT, you receive 1 BLURT (at most every 3 days).
rewards.lent_note: Lent BLURT Power adds to your voting weight on Blurt and stays the relay's.
